passages.text: Identification of amino acid residues critical for the interaction of fibrin with N-cadherin

We recently identified N-cadherin as a novel receptor for fibrin and localized complementary binding sites within the fibrin betaN-domains and the third and fifth extracellular domains (EC3 and EC5) of N-cadherin. We also hypothesized that the His16 and Arg17 residues of the betaN-domains and the (Asp/Glu)-X-(Asp/Glu) motifs present in the EC3 and EC5 domains may play a role in the interaction between fibrin and N-cadherin. The primary objectives of this study were to test these hypotheses and further clarify the structural basis for this interaction. To test our hypotheses, we first mutated His16 and Arg17 in the recombinant (beta15-66)2 fragment, which mimics the dimeric arrangement of the betaN-domains domains in fibrin, using site-directed mutagenesis. The results revealed that the mutation of both His16 and Arg17 is critical for the interaction. Next, we mutated Asp/Glu residues in the three (Asp/Glu)-X-(Asp/Glu) motifs, M1 (Asp-Phe-Glu), M2 (Glu-Ala-Glu), and M3 (Asp-Tyr-Asp), of the fibrin-binding N-cad(3-5) fragment of N-cadherin. The results showed that Asp292 and Glu294 of M1, and Asp468 and Asp470 of M3, are critical for the interaction. Our molecular modeling of the 3D structure of the EC3-EC4-EC5 domains revealed that these residues are located at the interfaces of EC3-EC4 and EC4-EC5 and some may also be involved in calcium binding. In conclusion, our study identified amino acid residues in the fibrin betaN-domains and the EC3 and EC5 domains of N-cadherin that are critical for the interaction of fibrin with N-cadherin and localized the fibrin binding residues in the 3D structure of N-cadherin.
INTRODUCTION

Fibrinogen is a multifunctional plasma protein that, upon conversion into polymeric fibrin, becomes highly reactive and interacts with various plasma proteins and cell types through their respective receptors. These interactions play a prominent role in several important physiological and pathological processes, including hemostasis, wound healing, thrombosis, atherogenesis, tumorigenesis, etc. In hemostasis, the thrombin-mediated conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin contributes to the formation of blood clots, which prevent blood loss caused by vascular injury. The highly reactive polymeric fibrin also serves as a scaffold to which fibrinolytic proteins, such as plasminogen and tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), bind, resulting in the activation of plasminogen into plasmin and subsequent dissolution of blood clots during fibrinolysis. Furthermore, fibrin participates in wound healing by promoting normal inflammation and angiogenesis. Specifically, fibrin contributes to inflammation through its interaction with the endothelial Very Low-Density Lipoprotein (VLDL) receptor. Fibrin also promotes angiogenesis through its interaction with Vascular Endothelial-cadherin (VE-cadherin). We recently discovered that fibrin also interacts with Neural-cadherin (N-cadherin). The pathophysiological role of this interaction is not yet established.

N-cadherin is a member of the cell adhesion cadherin superfamily and belongs to the classical cadherin family, which also includes VE-cadherin, P-cadherin, E-cadherins, and others. It is expressed by various cell types, including neural, endothelial, mesenchymal, and poorly differentiated cancer cells. In endothelial cells, N-cadherin is distributed over the entire cell membrane and may mediate interactions of these cells with other cell types. Specifically, it has been shown that N-cadherin mediates adhesion, recognition, and signaling between pericytes and endothelial cells, which are essential for normal vascular morphogenesis. It has also been shown that a soluble N-cadherin fragment promotes angiogenesis. Thus, N-cadherin plays a crucial role in vascular morphogenesis, contributing to the formation of blood vessels, and its deficiency in mice causes embryonic lethality. Furthermore, it promotes the metastatic behavior of tumor cells. N-cadherin is a transmembrane glycoprotein composed of five homologous extracellular domains, each encompassing approximately 110 amino acid residues, a transmembrane domain, and a cytoplasmic domain (Figure 1A). The extracellular domains of N-cadherin are primarily involved in cell-cell interactions and the regulation of intercellular adhesion. They also interact with fibrin, although the functional role of this interaction remains unclear.

The fibrinogen molecule consists of two identical subunits, each formed by three non-identical disulfide-linked polypeptide chains, Aalpha, Bbeta, and gamma, in which the letters A and B designate fibrinopeptides A and B (amino acid residues 1-16 and 1-14, respectively). The conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin occurs through thrombin-mediated proteolytic cleavage of these fibrinopeptides. The polypeptide chains in both fibrinogen and fibrin form more than 20 distinct domains, which are involved in numerous interactions with plasma proteins and cellular receptors. Specifically, the N-terminal portions of the fibrin beta chains form a pair of the betaN-domains, each encompassing amino acid residues 15-64 (Figure 1C). These domains are highly reactive, interacting with heparin, the VLDL receptor, VE-cadherin, and with the recently discovered novel receptor for fibrin, N-cadherin. Notably, the recombinant dimeric (beta15-66)2 fragment (Figure 1D), corresponding to these domains and mimicking their dimeric arrangement in fibrin, preserves the binding properties of fibrin to the abovementioned receptors.

While the pathophysiological role of the newly discovered interaction between fibrin and N-cadherin has not yet been established, understanding the structural basis for this interaction may clarify its functions. As the initial step in establishing this basis, we recently localized the N-cadherin-binding sites within the betaN-domains of fibrin and identified complementary fibrin-binding sites within the third and fifth extracellular domains of N-cadherin (Figure 1). The primary objective of the present study was to identify the critical amino acid residues in these domains that mediate the interaction of fibrin with N-cadherin.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Antibodies and Reagents.

The anti-His(C-term) monoclonal antibody (anti-His tag mAb) conjugated with HRP was from Invitrogen (Carlsbad, CA). The sheep anti-N-cadherin polyclonal antibodies AF6426 were purchased from R&D Systems (Minneapolis, MN). The horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated rabbit anti-sheep polyclonal antibodies and the SuperBlue Reserve TMB microwell peroxidase substrate were from SeraCare (Milfort, MA). Thrombin CleanCleave kit was obtained from Sigma (St. Louis, MO). Blocker BSA in TBS (10x) was from Thermo Scientific (Rockford, IL)
Preparation of the (beta15-66)2 Fragment and its Mutants.

The recombinant (beta15-66)2 fragment (Figure 1D) was prepared as described earlier. The dimeric (beta15-66)2 mutant fragments with single mutations, Mut-(beta18-66)2, Mut-(beta15-66)2-H16A, and Mut-(beta15-66)2-R17Q, were prepared according to the previously described procedures. Mut-(Bbeta1-66)-H16A,R17A, the monomeric Bbeta1-66 fragment ("B" indicates fibrinopeptide B including amino acid residues 1-14) with double mutations (His16Ala-Arg17Ala), was generated by site-directed mutagenesis using QuikChange Multi Site-Directed Mutagenesis kit (Stratagene, La Jolla, CA). The pCAL-n construct containing DNA encoding the fibrinogen Bbeta1-66 region was modified using the mutagenic primer shown in Table 1. The desired mutations were confirmed by sequencing mutant plasmid. The monomeric Mut-(Bbeta1-66)-H16A,R17A mutant fragment was produced in E. coli strain BL21(DE3), purified, and dimerized using procedures described earlier for the wild-type dimeric (beta15-66)2 fragment. The dimeric fibrinogen-related Mut-(Bbeta1-66)2-H16A,R17A mutant fragment was treated with thrombin-agarose from Thrombin CleanCleave kit using conditions described before to remove its fibrinopeptides B and to produce fibrin-related Mut-(beta15-66)2-H16A,R17A fragment. The purity of the resultant fragment was verified by SDS-PAGE analysis.
Preparation of the Recombinant N-cadherin Fragments.

Recombinant soluble N-cadherin fragment (sN-cadherin), which corresponds to the extracellular portion of N-cadherin including all five extracellular (EC) domains, and its recombinant fragment, N-cad(3-5), including EC domains 3-4-5 (Figure 1B), were prepared as described before.
Preparation of N-cad(3-5) Fragment Mutants.

For this study, we prepared three mutants of the N-cad(3-5) fragment in which Asp/Glu residues in each of the (Asp/Glu)-X-(Asp/Glu) motifs (Figure 2) were replaced with Ala. Specifically, Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M1-M2-M3 mutant fragment contained Asp292Ala and Glu294Ala mutations in motif M1, Glu450Ala and Glu452Ala in motif M2, and Asp468Ala and Asp470Ala in motif M3; Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M1-M3 fragment contained Asp292Ala and Glu294Ala mutations in motif M1, and Asp468Ala and Asp470Ala mutations in motif M3; and Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M2 fragment contained Glu450Ala and Glu452Ala mutations in motif M2. All three mutant fragments were generated by site-directed mutagenesis using QuikChange Multi Site-Directed Mutagenesis kit (Stratagene, La Jolla, CA). The pET20b construct containing DNA encoding the N-cad(3-5) fragment tagged with six His residues was modified using the mutagenic primers presented in Table 1. The desired mutations were confirmed by sequencing the mutant plasmids. The mutant fragments were produced in E. coli strain BL21(DE3)pLysS, and refolded and purified by the procedures described for the wild-type N-cad(3-5) fragment. The purity of the resultant mutant fragment was verified by SDS-PAGE analysis.
Surface Plasmon Resonance.

Interaction of the (beta15-66)2 and Mut-(beta18-66)2 fragments with immobilized sN-cadherin was studied by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) using the BIAcore 3000 biosensor (GE Healthcare), which measure association/dissociation of proteins in real time, as we described previously. The experiments were performed in 10 mM HEPES buffer, pH 7.4, containing 2 mM CaCl2, 0.15 M NaCl, and 0.005% Surfactant P20.
Solid-Phase Binding Assay.

The interaction of sN-cadherin with the (beta15-66)2 fragment and its mutants, as well as that of the N-cad(3-5) fragment and its mutants with (beta15-66)2, was evaluated using an Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA). In the ELISA experiments, wells of Immulon 2HB microtiter plates were coated overnight with (beta15-66)2 or its mutants at 2 mug/mL in 0.1 M Na2CO3, pH 9.5 (coating buffer) at 4  C. The wells were then blocked with Blocker BSA in TBS (20 mM Tris, pH 7.4, and 150 mM NaCl) for 1 hour at room temperature. Following washing with TBS containing 0.05% Tween 20, 2 mM CaCl2, and 0.1% BSA (ELISA-binding buffer), the indicated concentrations of sN-cadherin or N-cad(3-5) and its mutants in this buffer were added to the wells and to control wells coated just with Blocker BSA, and incubated overnight at 4  C. Bound sN-cadherin was detected by reaction with the primary anti-N-cadherin AF6426 polyclonal antibodies (1 hour at 37  C) and the secondary HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-sheep polyclonal antibodies (1 hour at 37  C). Bound N-cad(3-5) and its mutant fragments were detected by reaction with anti-His monoclonal antibody conjugated with HRP (1 hour at 37  C). The peroxidase substrate, SuperBlue Reserve TMB, was added to the wells, and the amount of bound ligand was measured spectrophotometrically at 450 nm. Data were analyzed by nonlinear regression analysis using the following equation: A = Amax/(1 + Kd/[L]), where A represents the absorbance of the oxidized substrate, which is assumed to be proportional to the amount of ligand bound, Amax is the absorbance at saturation, [L] is the molar concentration of the ligand, and Kd is the dissociation constant.
Fluorescence Spectroscopy.

Fluorescence spectra and thermal unfolding of the N-cad(3-5) fragment and its mutants were recorded in an SLM 8000-C fluorometer. Specifically, the spectra were recorded with excitation at 280 nm, and the thermal unfolding in the 10-95  C temperature range was measured by monitoring the ratio of fluorescence intensity at 370 nm to that at 330 nm with the same excitation, as we described earlier. The temperature was controlled with a circulating water bath. All experiments were performed in a 1 cm path-length quartz cuvette in TBS containing 2 mM CaCl2.
Molecular modeling.

Prediction of the structure for the three extracellular domains of N-cadherin (amino acid residues 217-551, see Figure 1B) was performed using AlphaFold2. Positions of calcium ions were taken from the structures of chicken VE-cadherin EC1-2 domains (PDB ID: 3PPE) and mouse cadherin-8 EC1-3 domains (PDB ID: 2A62). The representative model illustrating the proposed interaction between the (beta15-66)2 dimer and the N-cad(3-5) fragment was generated from a pair of predictions for the fibrin beta15-66 fragment against either the EC3-5 domains of N-cadherin (to generate an interaction with the DYD motif) or the EC3-4 domains (to generate an interaction with the DFE motif), using Alphafold Server. The EC4 domains of each prediction were then aligned and positioned near an AlphaFold prediction of two fibrin beta15-66 fragments without N-cadherin to serve as a template for their C-terminal association. The predictions were then merged in PayMOL (The PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 1.5.03 Schrodinger, LLC; 2012) by rebuilding the region from residues 25-53 of each fragment using the LDRS function in the software package IDPConformerGenerator.
RESULTS
Identification of amino acid residues in fibrin that are critical for its interaction with N-cadherin.

Our previous study revealed that the dimeric recombinant (beta15-66)2 fragment, which mimics a pair of the fibrin betaN-domains (Figure 1C and D), interacts with VE-cadherin with high affinity. We also found that the mutation of its amino acid residues, His16 or Arg17, abrogates this interaction, indicating that these two residues are critical for its binding to VE-cadherin. Since the (beta15-66)2 fragment interacts with both VE-cadherin and N-cadherin, which are structurally homologous, we hypothesized that His16 and Arg17 of this fragment may also be involved in the interaction of fibrin with N-cadherin. To test this hypothesis, the following experiments have been performed.

First, we tested the interaction of the truncated mutant fragment, Mut-(beta18-66)2, which lacks the N-terminal Gly15-His16-Arg17 residues, with a soluble form of N-cadherin, sN-cadherin. In SPR experiments, the control (beta15-66)2 fragment, added at 25 nM to immobilized sN-cadherin, exhibited prominent binding, as expected (Figure 3). In contrast, Mut-(beta18-66)2 failed to bind even at 100 nM, a concentration 8-fold higher than the Kd of 12.5 nM determined for the interaction of sN-cadherin with (beta15-66)2. This finding was confirmed in ELISA experiments, in which sN-cadherin added at increasing concentrations to immobilized (beta15-66)2 exhibited prominent binding, while Mut-(beta18-66)2 failed to bind even at 200 nM (Figure 4). Next, we performed similar ELISA experiments with the Mut-(beta15-66)2-H16A and Mut-(beta15-66)2-R17Q mutant fragments, in which His16 and Arg17 residues were replaced with Ala and Gln, respectively, as well as with the double mutant, Mut-(beta15-66)2-H16A,R17A, in which both residues, His16 and Arg17, were mutated to Ala. The results obtained revealed that the mutation of either of these two residues significantly reduced binding of sN-cadherin to the (beta15-66)2 mutants, while mutation of both residues effectively abrogated this binding (Figure 4). Altogether, these experiments clearly indicate that both His16 and Arg17 residues of the (beta15-66)2 fragment are critical for the interaction of fibrin with sN-cadherin, confirming our hypothesis.
Ionic strength dependence of the interaction between (beta15-66)2 and N-cadherin.

The involvement of the positively charged Arg17 residue of the (beta15-66)2 fragment in its binding to sN-cadherin suggests that electrostatic interactions may play a role in the interaction of fibrin with N-cadherin. To test this suggestion, we performed a systematic study, in which increasing concentrations of the N-cad(3-5) fragment, which contains both fibrin-binding domains, EC3 and EC5, were added to the immobilized (beta15-66)2 fragment at different concentrations of NaCl, using ELISA. The results obtained clearly indicate that the binding affinity of this interaction is ionic strength dependent. Specifically, The Kd values for this interaction were increased from 69 to 367 nM with increasing NaCl concentration from 0.15 to 0.25 M NaCl, and the interaction was completely abrogated at 0.5 and 1.0 M NaCl (Figure 5). Thus, this finding confirms that the electrostatic interactions between the positively charged Arg residue of (beta15-66)2 and, most probably, the negatively charged Asp/Glu residues of the EC3 and EC5 domains are involved in the interaction of fibrin with N-cadherin.
Identification of amino acid residues in N-cadherin that are critical for its interaction with fibrin.

Our previous study localized the fibrin-binding sites within the third and fifth extracellular domains of N-cadherin (EC3 and EC5 domains, respectively). Furthermore, in our previous study, based on the sequence analysis of N-cadherin and VE-cadherin and some assumptions, we hypothesized that the (Asp/Glu)-X-(Asp/Glu) motif, which is present in both the EC3 and EC5 domains of N-cadherin (Figure 2), may be involved in the interaction with fibrin. This hypothesis is in agreement with the results of our experiments described above (Figure 5), suggesting the involvement of the Arg residue of (beta15-66)2 and the Asp/Glu residues of the N-cad(3-5) fragment in the interaction between fibrin and N-cadherin. The following experiments have been performed to test this hypothesis.

According to our hypothesis, there are three (Asp/Glu)-X-(Asp/Glu) motifs in N-cadherin, Asp-Phe-Glu (DFE or M1) in the EC3 domain, and Glu-Ala-Glu (EAE or M2) and Asp-Tyr-Asp (DYD or M3) in the EC5 domain (Figure 2), that may be involved in the interaction with fibrin. They all contain two closely spaced negatively charged Asp/Glu residues. To test this hypothesis, we replace these Asp/Glu residues in all three motifs with Ala using site-directed mutagenesis (see Materials and Methods). The mutagenesis was performed with the N-cad(3-5) fragment containing both fibrin-binding extracellular domains, EC3 and EC5. Among mutants obtained, one contained the desired mutations in all three motifs, M1, M2, and M3, the other one contained the desired mutations in M1 and M3, and the third one contained such mutations only in the M2 motif. These mutans, Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M1-M2-M3, Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M1-M3, and Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M2, were selected for subsequent experiments.

Since the recombinant mutant fragments were expressed in E. coli and refolded from denaturing buffer containing 6 M GdmCl, we first confirmed the folding status of these fragments using fluorescence spectroscopy. They all exhibited fluorescence spectra with maximum at 340 nm, like that of the wild-type N-cad(3-5) fragment (Figure 6, inset), which is characteristic of folded proteins. Furthermore, when heated in the fluorimeter while monitoring the ratio of fluorescence intensity at 370 nm to that at 330 nm, they all displayed sigmoidal unfolding transitions (Figure 6), further confirming that they all are folded into compact structures similar to that of the wild-type N-cad(3-5) fragment.

Next, we tested the interaction of these mutant fragments with the (beta15-66)2 fragment using ELISA. When increasing concentrations of the Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M1-M2-M3, Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M1-M3, and Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M2 fragments were added to immobilized (beta15-66)2, the first two exhibited practically no binding (Figure 7). In contrast, the binding of the Mut-N-cad(3-5)-M2 fragment was comparable to that of the control wild-type N-cad(3-5) fragment. Altogether, these experiments confirm our hypothesis that the Asp/Glu residues of the (Asp/Glu)-X-(Asp/Glu) motif in the EC3 and EC5 domains of N-cadherin play a critical role in the interaction with fibrin. They also indicate that the M2 motif in the EC5 domain is not involved in this interaction.
Location of the M1 and M3 fibrin-binding motifs in N-cadherin.

Having identified the amino acid residues in N-cadherin that are critical for its interaction with fibrin, we can now evaluate their location within the N-cadherin structure. Since the 3D structure of human N-cadherin has not yet been established, we performed molecular modelling of the structure of its EC3, EC4, and EC5 domains, two of which are involved in fibrin binding, using the AlphaFold tool (see Materials and Methods). The resulting model (Figure 8A) revealed that the M1 (DFE) and M3 (DYD) fibrin-binding motifs are positioned within loop structures located at the inter-domain EC3-EC4 and EC4-EC5 interfaces and are exposed for interaction with fibrin. In contrast, the non-fibrin-binding M2 (EAE) motif of the EC5 domain, which is also well-exposed for interaction, is located on a stable beta-strand, away from the EC4-EC5 interface. This observation raises the question of why the M2 motif is not involved in the interaction with fibrin.
DISCUSSION

In our previous study, we discovered that N-cadherin serves as a novel receptor for fibrin. As an initial step towards elucidating the structural basis for the interaction between fibrin and N-cadherin, we localized the fibrin-binding sites within the third and fifth extracellular domains of N-cadherin (EC3 and EC5 domains, respectively), along with the complementary N-cadherin-binding sites within the fibrin betaN-domains. In the present study, we further clarified the structural basis for this interaction by identifying the amino acid residues in both fibrin and N-cadherin that are critical for their interaction.

Our hypothesis that the His16 and Arg17 residues of the fibrin betaN-domains may be involved in the interaction of fibrin with N-cadherin is based on the structural similarity between N-cadherin and VE-cadherin, both of which interact with fibrin, as well as on our previous finding that these residues are critical for the interaction of fibrin with VE-cadherin. Consequently, our ELISA experiments aimed at identifying the fibrin betaN-domain residues involved in the interaction with N-cadherin, were performed using previously prepared single mutant fragments, Mut-(beta15-66)2-H16A and Mut-(beta15-66)2-R17Q. These experiments revealed that mutation of either His16 or Arg17 significantly, but not completely, reduced the interaction of the mutant fragments with sN-cadherin. Therefore, we expressed a new double mutant, Mut-(beta15-66)2-H16A,R17A, in which both His16 and Arg17 residues were replaced with Ala, and performed similar ELISA experiments. The results obtained with the double mutant revealed that mutation of these two residues resulted in a complete loss of its ability to bind sN-cadherin (Figure 4). These results clearly indicate that both His16 and Arg17 residues of the fibrin betaN-domains are critical for the interaction of fibrin with N-cadherin. Nevertheless, they do not exclude the potential contributions of other betaN-domain residues to this interaction.

To identify residues in N-cadherin that are critical for its interaction with fibrin, we utilized our previous hypothesis, which suggests that the (Asp/Glu)-X-(Asp/Glu) motif, present in both the EC3 and EC5 domains of N-cadherin, may be involved in this interaction. This hypothesis is based on two major assumptions discussed in our previous publication. First, that the interaction of fibrin with the EC3 domain of N-cadherin and with the EC3 domain of VE-cadherin may occur similarly, involving the same or homologous amino acid residues. Second, that the interaction of the fibrin beta chain residues, particularly Arg17, with the EC3 and EC5 domains of N-cadherin may resemble the interaction of the Gly15-His-Arg17-containing knob "B" (see Figure 1C), which represents the secondary polymerization site and contains this residue, with the complementary hole "b" in the fibrin D region. According to a previous report, this interaction, which plays an important role in the fibrin polymerization process, primarily occurs through the closely spaced negatively charged Glu397 and Asp398 of hole "b". To test our hypothesis, we mutated Asp/Glu residues in the (Asp/Glu)-X-(Asp/Glu) motifs of the N-cad(3-5) fragment, which contains both fibrin-binding domains, EC3 and EC5. The results revealed that these mutations completely abrogate the interaction between fibrin and N-cadherin (Figure 7), thereby confirming our hypothesis.

Our hypothesis predicts the presence of three (Asp/Glu)-X-(Asp/Glu) motifs in the EC3 and EC5 domains (Figure 2) that may be involved in the interaction with fibrin. However, our experiments revealed that only two of these motifs, M1 and M3, participate in fibrin binding, while M2 does not. This finding indicates that Asp292 and Glu294 of the M1 motif and Asp468 and Asp470 of the M3 motif are critical for the interaction of N-cadherin with fibrin. The key difference between the M1 and M3 motifs compared to M2 is the presence of an aromatic amino acid residue between Glu/Asp in the former, while there is an Ala residue in between the two Asp residues in the latter. This strongly suggests that the aromatic residues in the M1 and M3 motifs, Phe293 and Tyr469, are also involved in the interaction with fibrin. Further structural studies are required to test this suggestion.

It is well established that the adhesive properties of cadherins depend on calcium ions, with their calcium-binding amino acid residues primarily located between their extracellular domains. Since the negatively charged Glu/Asp residues of the fibrin-binding M1 and M3 motifs are also located at the EC3-EC4 and EC4-EC5 domain interfaces (Figure 8A), we performed molecular modeling to assess whether these residues might also be involved in calcium binding. To approximate the positioning of Ca2+ at these interfaces, we used the known X-ray structures of the extracellular domains of chicken VE-cadherin and mouse cadherin-8 with bound calcium ions. Molecular modeling revealed that the Glu294 residue in DFE of the EC3 domain (Figure 8B) and the Asp470 residue in DYD of the EC5 domain (Figure 8C) might serve as calcium ligands. However, these two residues are critical for the interaction of N-cadherin with fibrin, as discussed above. Furthermore, our previous study revealed that the interaction between fibrin and N-cadherin is independent of calcium binding. The most probable explanation for this discrepancy is that Glu294 and Asp470 may switch from Ca2+ binding to the interaction with the fibrin betaN-domains upon the binding of fibrin to N-cadherin. In support of this speculation, a similar switch from calcium binding to ligand interaction has been previously reported for the interaction of the Gly-His-Arg-Pro peptide, which mimics polymerization knob "B", with the complementary hole "b". Specifically, analysis of the crystal structures of the fibrinogen D fragment with and without Gly-His-Arg-Pro revealed that Asp398 of hole "b" is involved in the interaction with Ca2+ in the absence of this peptide and flips to interact with this peptide in its presence. Further structural studies are required to test our speculation.

It should be noted that the structure of the fibrin betaN-domains has not yet been established. Although these domains may be compact in fibrinogen and unfolded in fibrin, our previous study revealed that the structure of these domains in the recombinant (beta15-66)2 fragment is disordered. In this disordered conformation, the His16-Arg17 residues, located at the N-termini of the (beta15-66)2 dimer and disulfide-linked by Cys65 (see Figure 1D), may extend at least 32 nm from each other, a distance greater than that between the fibrin-binding DFE and DYD motifs in the model shown in Figure 8A. This suggests that each monomer of the dimeric (beta15-66)2 fragment, as well as the two fibrin betaN-domains, may interact with one N-cadherin molecule or one N-cad(3-5) fragment, with one monomer binding to the EC3 domain and the other one to the EC5 domain, forming a 1:1 complex. The results of modeling such a complex are presented in Figure 9. Further studies are required to confirm this mode of interaction.
CONCLUSION

In summary, the present study identified critical amino acid residues involved in the interaction between fibrin and its novel receptor, N-cadherin. These include the His16 and Arg17 residues of the fibrin betaN-domains, as well as the Asp292 and Glu294 residues of the M1 motif (Asp-Phe-Glu) and the Asp468 and Asp470 residues of the M3 motif (Asp-Tyr-Asp) located in the EC3 and EC5 domains of N-cadherin, respectively. Our molecular modeling localized the key fibrin-binding Asp/Glu residues within the structure of the EC3 and EC5 domains of N-cadherin and revealed their relationship to Ca2+ binding. Identifying these critical residues not only enhances our understanding of the structural basis for the interaction of fibrin with N-cadherin, but may also help in clarifying the functional role for this interaction. In our previous study, we suggested that the fibrin-(N-cadherin) interaction may play a role in angiogenesis. If confirmed, this interaction may serve as a potential target for regulating fibrin-dependent angiogenesis.

passages.text: Life Course Considerations in Environmental Health: Developmental Neurotoxicity of Domoic Acid at Doses Below Acute Effect Levels in Adult Humans
ABSTRACT
Background

Current US federal action levels for domoic acid (DA) in seafood are based on acute toxicity observed in exposed adult humans. Life course considerations have not been incorporated. The potential for developmental neurotoxicity (DNT) at permissible DA levels has previously been noted, but not methodically assessed.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Methods

Studies of DNT following DA exposure in experimental and wild animals were identified through a comprehensive search strategy. Evidence from papers meeting inclusion criteria was evaluated for specific outcomes reported for doses at which adverse effects were observed. Exposure levels associated with DNT were compared with those known to cause adult toxicity. The findings are discussed in the context of the well-characterized mechanism of DA neurotoxicity, as well as the toxicokinetics of DA across species and life stages.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Conclusions

DNT outcomes were reported with a no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) 10 times lower than the NOAEL of 0.75 mg DA/kg for acute effects in adults. Apart from reviewing current regulatory action levels, public health outreach messaging to health care professionals and sensitive populations, such as pregnant or breastfeeding women, should be considered as a means of increasing awareness about risk for DNT from consumption of potentially DA-contaminated seafood.
Introduction

Many researchers have expressed concerns as to whether current safety considerations for the presence of domoic acid (DA) in seafood are sufficient to protect individual consumers throughout the course of their lives (Costa, Giordano, and Faustman ; Doucette and Tasker ; Grattan ; Panlilio et al. ; Petroff et al. ; Shum et al. ). The sensitivity of age-based sub-populations can vary due to the developmental stage of target tissues (e.g., brain), as well as with life-stage changes in toxicokinetic (TK) factors such as rates of absorption and elimination (Lanphear ).

Compared to the adult brain, developing brains are generally more sensitive to the effects of neurotoxicants (Costa, Guizzetti, and Vitalone ; Lanphear ; Rodier ). Prenatal and early postnatal brain development are characterized by rapid neural cell proliferation and migration, maturation of receptor and transmitter systems, increasing numbers of synaptic connections, and production of myelin (Rodier ). Interference with any of these essential developmental processes can adversely impact eventual mature brain structure and/or function (Costa, Guizzetti, and Vitalone ). Simultaneously, an immature blood-brain barrier may not provide the developing brain with the same degree of protection from circulating toxins as afforded to an adult brain by a mature barrier (Costa, Guizzetti, and Vitalone ; Rodier ).

The neurotoxic effects of DA are consistent among adults of the species evaluated including humans, laboratory animals, and affected wildlife (Goldstein et al. ; Grant et al. ; Iverson and Truelove ). Experimental evidence indicates that developing brains are more sensitive than adult brains to DA-induced neurotoxicity (Costa, Giordano, and Faustman ; Petroff et al. ).

For this commentary, we have compiled the empirical evidence from studies of DA-induced developmental neurotoxicity (DNT) in experimental and wild animals. Specific impacts observed at the lowest DA doses with an adverse effect were compared across species and developmental stages. While the exact timing of key neurodevelopmental events with respect to the pre- versus post-natal periods may vary among species (Clancy et al. ), the sequence of events appears to be highly conserved (Clancy, Darlington, and Finlay ). The results are discussed in the context of available background information on mechanisms of DA neurotoxicity and the TK of DA at various life stages. The detailed information presented in this commentary will be valuable for communicating risks of DA exposure throughout life.
Sources of DA Exposure

DA is a potent neurotoxin produced by algal diatoms. On the west coast of the US (OEHHA ; Petroff et al. ) and in many other jurisdictions worldwide (Bates et al. ), diatoms of the genus Pseudo-nitzschia are the most common source. Shellfish and fish can accumulate DA by feeding in waters contaminated with DA-containing cells of Pseudo-nitzschia (Bernstein et al. ; Lefebvre, Frame, and Kendrick ; Lefebvre et al. ). Accumulated DA can then be passed on to higher trophic levels (OEHHA ) including seabirds (Gibble et al. ), marine mammals (Bowen et al. ; Goldstein et al. ; Kreuder ; Moriarty et al. ), and humans (Fritz et al. ).
Acute Effects of DA (1987 Amnesic Shellfish Poisoning Outbreak)

The acute effects of DA poisoning in adults came to wide attention following a 1987 outbreak involving over 100 people who consumed cultured mussels sourced from eastern Prince Edward Island, Canada (Perl, Bedard, Kosatsky, Hockin, Todd, Remis, et al. ). Symptoms ranged from gastrointestinal (GI) distress, to disorientation, seizure, coma, and death (Perl, Bedard, Kosatsky, Hockin, Todd, Remis, et al. ). DA poisoning is also referred to as "Amnesic Shellfish Poisoning" (ASP) because temporary or permanent loss of short-term memory is a characteristic symptom at higher exposure levels (Grant et al. ; Perl, Teitelbaum, et al. ; Teitelbaum et al. ).

Ingested doses of DA were estimated for 10 individuals from the 1987 outbreak based on DA concentrations in meal remnants and estimated portions consumed (Perl, Bedard, Kosatsky, Hockin, Todd, Remis, et al. ). A single individual estimated to have consumed 20 mg of DA had no adverse GI or neurological effects (EFSA ). With doses normalized to 60 kg body weight (bw), the lowest observed adverse effect level (LOAEL) was determined to be 1.0 mg DA/kg bw, which was associated with mild gastrointestinal effects (Iverson and Truelove ). Severe illness requiring hospitalization was associated with an estimated dose of 4 mg DA/kg bw (EFSA ; Perl, Bedard, Kosatsky, Hockin, Todd, Remis, et al. ).
Basic Mechanism of Action (Kainic Acid Analog)

DA is a high-affinity structural analog of kainic acid (Figure 1), and hence a selective agonist of kainate receptors (a subtype of ionotropic glutamate receptors) (Larm, Beart, and Cheung ). At sufficient concentrations, agonists of glutamate receptors can over-stimulate neurons to death in a process known as excitotoxicity. Excitotoxicity contributes to impairment of learning and memory as well as to frank neurodegeneration in the hippocampus and neocortex (AOP-48 ; Larm, Beart, and Cheung ). DA has a higher affinity for kainate receptors than kainic acid itself, resulting in 3-20 fold greater potency for downstream effects (Larm, Beart, and Cheung ; Costa, Giordano, and Faustman ).
Chemical structures of domoic acid, and analogues glutamic acid and kainic acid.

The Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) for ionotropic glutamate receptors in adult brain (Figure 2) illustrates the sequence of key events from receptor binding through apical expression as deficits in learning and memory (AOP-48 ). The AOP is intended to apply to all types of glutamate ionotropic receptors, including kainate receptors, involved in basal excitatory synaptic transmission and synaptic plasticity, which under physiological conditions are critical for normal learning and memory. DA's action as an agonist for glutamate receptors is sufficiently well-understood and specific to support its use as a positive control for certain in vitro assays used in large-scale screening of compounds for potential DNT (USEPA ). While not specifically validated for developing brains, current evidence tends to support the pathway's applicability (AOP-48 ).

Schematic diagram of the adverse outcome pathway (AOP) for domoic acid and similar compounds. Modified from the AOP "Binding of agonists to ionotropic glutamate receptors in adult brain leading to excitotoxicity that mediates neuronal cell death, contributing to learning and memory impairment" (AOP 48, 2023) available online at: https://aopwiki.org/aops/48.

Data from humans, mice, and rats used to construct the AOP were characterized as strong evidence (AOP-48 ). Binding of DA to ionotropic glutamate receptors and the resulting adverse neurological effects have been documented broadly in additional vertebrate species including non-human primates, marine mammals, birds, and finfish (Lefebvre, Frame, and Kendrick ; Lefebvre et al. ; Lefebvre ). While fish treated with DA by injection are susceptible to DA-caused excitotoxicity, they may be less sensitive to oral doses of DA when compared to other species (Anderson et al. ; Lefebvre, Frame, and Kendrick ; Lefebvre et al. ; Lefebvre ). Fish die-offs have not been observed to result from Pseudo-nitzschia blooms, even when DA levels in fish digestive tract tissues were high (e.g., > 50 mg DA/kg viscera) (Bernstein et al. ; Lefebvre, Frame, and Kendrick ; Lefebvre et al. ).

Ionotropic glutamate receptors, including kainate receptors, have also been identified in tissues of the GI tract (Baj et al. ). These receptors are part of the "microbiota-gut-brain axis," and modulation of their activity may influence brain as well as gut function. While vomiting and other GI effects have been reported from DA exposure in humans and non-human primates, the specific involvement of ionotropic glutamate receptors in these symptoms has not been definitively established.
Basic Toxicokinetics (TK) of DA

DA is poorly absorbed from the GI tract, and is rapidly eliminated (e.g., half-life < 110 min reported for non-human primates) with approximately 75% metabolically unchanged in urine and feces (Suzuki and Hierlihy ; Truelove and Iverson ; Truelove et al. ; Jing et al. ; Costa, Giordano, and Faustman ). Distribution and elimination of DA has been studied in pregnant and non-pregnant animals (Jing et al. ; Maucher Fuquay et al. ; Shum et al. ), as well as in fetuses and neonates (Maucher Fuquay et al. ; Maucher and Ramsdell ).

The results from TK studies of acutely dosed DA differ between the injection and oral routes of exposure. In adult female cynomolgus monkeys ( Macaca fascicularis ), a single intravenous (IV) dose of 5 mug DA/kg bw (0.005 mg/kg) had a mean elimination half-life of 1.2 h (Jing et al. ). Acute oral doses of 0.075 and 0.15 mg DA/kg bw produced a mean terminal half-life of 11.3 h with the difference between routes indicating "flip-flop kinetics," or a rate of oral absorption that is slower than the rate of elimination and hence rate-limiting (Jing et al. ).

The TK of chronic oral dosing with DA at 0.075 and 0.15 mg/kg bw was studied in adult female cynomolgus monkeys before, during, and after pregnancy (Shum et al. ). At the time of delivery, DA was detected in infant plasma and amniotic fluid. TK modeling of maternal-fetal DA disposition suggested that placental transport introduces DA to the fetus via cord blood. The fetus subsequently eliminates DA into the amniotic fluid, which is then recirculated by fetal swallowing (Figure 3). DA levels were 4.5-7.5X higher in amniotic fluid than in fetal plasma, suggesting that DA accumulates in amniotic fluid.

Schematic diagram of maternal-fetal distribution of domoic acid (DA). DA in the maternal circulation is transported across the placenta and into the fetus via the umbilical vein. The fetal circulatory system transports DA to the immature fetal organs, including brain. The fetus eliminates DA into the amniotic fluid, which is swallowed by the fetus, thus recirculating available DA.

Distribution of DA in maternal and fetal tissues following gestational dosing is broadly consistent in experimental rats and monkeys (Maucher Fuquay et al. ; Shum et al. ), as well as in samples collected from fetal tissues and fluids of stranded sea lions (Brodie et al. ; Goldstein et al. ; Lefebvre et al. ). Following treatment of pregnant rats on gestation day (GD) 20 with 1.0 mg DA/kg bw IV, DA levels in maternal brain and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) peaked at 15 min following treatment and were undetectable by 12-24 h (Maucher Fuquay et al. ). Fetal plasma DA levels peaked at 60 min post-dosing (Maucher Fuquay et al. ). Post-treatment DA levels in amniotic fluid and fetal brain did not show evidence of elimination over 24 h. Retention of DA in the amniotic fluid of these experimental animals (Maucher Fuquay et al. ) reinforces the suggestion of continuous fetal re-exposure, in turn increasing the relative risk for fetal harm from a given maternal dose of DA.

Experiments in lactating rats demonstrated the presence of DA in the milk of treated dams and in the plasma of nursing pups given supplemental milk with added DA (Maucher and Ramsdell ). While at one-hour post-dosing with 1.0 mg/kg bw DA by intraperitoneal injection (IP) DA levels were 16 times lower in milk than in maternal plasma; by 8 h post-dosing, remaining DA levels were four times higher in milk than in maternal plasma. Although neonates given milk from these DA-exposed females that did not attain measurable plasma levels of DA, neonates did absorb sufficient DA from consuming milk "spiked" with 1.0 mg DA/kg bw to result in measurable plasma DA levels.
Current Basis for US Regulation of DA in Seafood

Health Canada was the first entity to establish and implement an official regulatory limit of 20 mug DA/g (20 ppm) for DA in edible tissue of bivalve shellfish in 1989. Prior to that, Canadian health and regulatory entities had instituted an interim safety threshold in 1988 that restricted shellfish harvest when DA levels exceeded 20 mug DA/g (Todd ; Wekell, Hurst, and Lefebvre ). Health Canada organized a symposium on DA toxicity in Ottawa (April 1989), where scientists, health officials, and regulators met to discuss various facets of the 1987 DA poisoning event, define the acute DA toxicity clinical syndrome now known as ASP, and establish the scientific basis for a safe consumption threshold for DA in shellfish of 20 ppm. Health Canada applied a LOAEL approach to calculate the threshold where 50 mg DA was divided by an approximate 0.200 kg (wet weight) shellfish consumption rate, or 250 ppm, to which a safety factor of 12 was applied (Perl, Bedard, Kosatsky, Hockin, Todd, Remis, et al. ; Perl, Bedard, Kosatsky, Hockin, Todd, McNutt, et al. ; Perl, Teitelbaum, et al. ; Todd ; Wekell, Hurst, and Lefebvre ).

passages.text: US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) critically reviewed the Health Canada regulatory limit at the FDA Pacific Region 1992 Domoic Acid Workshop in San Pedro, California, which was modeled after the 1989 Canadian symposium (DHHS ; USFDA ; Wekell, Hurst, and Lefebvre ). US FDA adopted the LOAEL approach using 60 mg DA as a LOAEL, divided by 0.250 kg (wet weight) shellfish consumption rate, or 240 ppm, and applied an uncertainty factor (UF) of 10. Twenty ppm was subsequently adopted and implemented as the FDA action level for DA in seafood (DHHS ). US FDA later evaluated additional DA data in Dungeness Crab and adopted a second action level in 1993 permitting 30 ppm DA in Dungeness Crab viscera (DHHS ; USFDA ).

Subsequent to the adoption of federal action limits, the Washington State Department of Health (DOH) conducted a literature review to determine a tolerable daily intake (TDI) for DA (Marien ). Overall, Washington DOH determined that the human and nonhuman primate toxicity data supported a no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) of 0.75 mg DA/ kg bw for acute exposure of adult individuals (Marien ). Due to the similarities between humans and test monkeys in response to doses of DA (Iverson and Truelove ), no between-species uncertainty factor (UF) was applied. Washington State health officials established a TDI of 0.075 mg DA/kg bw that incorporated a 10-fold UF to account for variation in sensitivity within species (Marien ). Washington DOH concluded that the TDI was consistent with the US FDA action levels of 30 and 20 ppm for crab viscera and clams, respectively, and that the federal limits were sufficiently protective of public health from acute DA toxicity.

passages.text: California State Agency Activities Regarding DA

The Office of Environmental and Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) is the lead California agency for evaluating health hazards posed by environmental contaminants and partners with other State agencies to ensure the safety of California fisheries from toxic substances, including DA (OEHHA ). As Pseudo-nitzschia blooms in California coastal waters are an ongoing concern, OEHHA assesses monitoring data for DA levels in California seafood samples analyzed by the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) laboratories. In consultation with CDPH, OEHHA makes formal health-based recommendations to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) regarding delay of opening, closure, or re-opening actions for California recreational and commercial fisheries under the authority of California Fish and Game Code section 5523 (CDFW) .

OEHHA, CDPH, and CDFW coordinate DA-related regulatory actions and provide the public with information in the form of responses to frequently asked questions (CDPH ; OEHHA ). These three entities, in cooperation with the California State Water Resources Control Board, comprise the Interagency harmful algal bloom (HAB)-related Illness Workgroup which investigates and tracks potential HAB-related illnesses in humans and animals throughout California, including DA-induced ASP, which is a reportable illness in California (OEHHA ). OEHHA has hosted two informational workshops on DA toxicity (2017 and 2019), which featured invited speakers from the research community (OEHHA ).

passages.text: Empirical Data: Implications for DA-Related DNT Risk

The extensive background information on DA summarized above affirms that life stage considerations are relevant to risk for DA's adverse neurological effects. Developing vertebrates are at particular risk of DA-induced DNT due to the immaturity of developing brain tissues. Developing mammals face the additional complexities of placental transfer, recirculation between the fetus and amniotic fluid with slow elimination from the amniotic fluid, and potential postnatal exposure via milk from exposed maternal animals.

An earlier review reported on experimental evidence for DNT occurring at DA doses one to two orders of magnitude below levels causing neurotoxicity in adults (Costa, Giordano, and Faustman ). This present effort compiles and summarizes the currently available experimental data on the developmental toxicity of DA in developing nonhuman animals. Taking a comprehensive look at dose-response data for DNT associated with DA exposure early in life for several species will facilitate considerations of whether the current action levels provide protection during the most sensitive life stages.

passages.text: Methods
Literature Identification and Selection
Search Strategies

The literature search strategy for prioritization candidates is detailed in a 2020 report by OEHHA (OEHHA ). The studies retrieved and reviewed for that document provided an initial nucleus for the DNT data presented in Tables.

The literature search for DA has been updated, and relevant new publications retrieved for inclusion. Additional efforts to identify relevant literature have included cross-checking reference lists from published papers, and author-based searches for papers published by researchers known to have worked on the DNT of DA.
Inclusion Criteria for Laboratory and Wild Animal Studies
Original data.
At least one dose level of DA plus appropriate controls.

Single or repeated DA dosing restricted to the pre- and/or postnatal periods of brain development, with specific timing reported to differentiate between DNT and adult neurotoxicity resulting from acute or chronic DA exposures of mature subjects.
Assessment and reporting of DNT outcomes such as behavioral, histopathological, and/or biochemical effects.

DNT assessment must have occurred subsequent to DA dosing; while timing of dosing is restrictive to the period of neurodevelopment, assessment of DNT outcomes could have been conducted at any time following dosing, from immediately post-dosing until later in life.
Laboratory studies included in the data tables met the following criteria by reporting:

For wild marine mammals, only rough estimates of dosing and timing of DA exposure could be made. Tabulated studies reported data on young animals believed to have been exposed during the prenatal and/or neonatal (nursing) periods. All of the selected literature reported on California sea lions found stranded, with DA exposure inferred from the timing and extent of known toxigenic Pseudo-nitzschia blooms capable of, or actively producing, DA (Smith et al. ). Some studies measured DA concentrations in affected animals' tissues and body fluids.
Results

Tables 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 summarize methods and results from whole-animal studies of DNT in DA-exposed animals. Each table represents studies grouped by time of exposure and species tested. Emphasis is placed on identifying the lowest dose at which DNT was observed for each study, and the specific effects reported at that dose. Where necessary to facilitate comparison between studies, units have been converted to mg/kg bw. Brief synopses of the tabulated information are presented below.
Prenatal Exposure
Monkey

Two publications reported on a single study population of  M. fascicularis  that was exposed to DA during gestation, and followed from birth to 1-2 months of age (Burbacher et al. ; Grant et al. ). Maternal animals were given DA orally, with doses of 0, 0.075, or 0.15 mg/kg-day throughout breeding and gestation. No adverse effects were noted for newborns, but testing at 1-2 months postnatal age revealed impairment of recognition memory in the 0.15 mg DA/kg bw-day group (Burbacher et al. ; Grant et al. ). See Table 1 for more details of study methods and results.
Gestational exposure only; Non-human primates ( Macaca fascicularis ).

ReferenceSpecies and populationOutcomes observed
Krucik et al. 2023

California sea lion: case study of a stranded, malnourished 7-month old California sea lion.

Not able to be permanently released, the animal was raised and cared for in captivity.

Exposure suspected to have occurred prenatally and/or pre-weaning.

Observations noted during the life of this animal were considered consistent with a hypothesis of early-life environmental DA exposure associated with adult-onset medial temporal lobe epilepsy.
Simeone et al. 2019

California sea lions with presumed exposure to DA were cared for at marine mammal centers.

Study population of 171 animals (all ages) determined to be unsuitable for release.

Neurological symptoms were significantly more likely among neonates than other age groups. The most common symptom was seizure.

Of eight neonates dying during the study, six exhibited neurological disease. Five of these six were necropsied, with 3/5 showing central nervous system and/or hippocampal lesions; one of these three showed hippocampal-focused encephalitis attributed specifically to DA toxicosis.

Goldstein et al. 2009

California sea lions on San Miguel Island, California.

Biological samples were analyzed for DA content, as well as for other contaminants and infectious diseases, in a study population of 67 aborted and live-born premature pups. Histopathology studies were conducted on various tissue samples (e.g., brain, placenta).

DA-producing algae were present in the environment and in sea lion feces.

DA was detected in biological fluid samples from 15/79 of tested pups.

Brain edema was observed in 6/9 prematurely born pups with detectable DA levels in the absence of other significant brain lesions.

2/5 placentas available for examination contained detectable levels of DA. Both had evidence of placental abruption.

Goldstein et al. 2008

Rescued California sea lions of all ages were studied while under care at The Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito, CA.

In-life symptoms of neurotoxicity were recorded and deceased animals were necropsied.

DA exposure was not always documented by tissue analysis, but inferred from environmental conditions (i.e., Pseudo-nitzschia bloom) at the time of rescue.

19 immature animals (1 pup, 3 yearlings, and 15 juveniles or subadults) exhibiting chronic neurological symptoms died in captivity. Symptoms included seizures and severe behavioral abnormalities.

Brain lesions noted among these animals included hemorrhage, edema, and mild meningoencephalitis in parahippocampal regions.

Symptoms included seizures and severe behavioral abnormalities.Brain lesions noted among these animals included hemorrhage, edema, and mild meningoencephalitis in parahippocampal regions.
Rodents

One study in rats (Levin et al. ) and five in mice (Dakshinamurti et al. ; Mills et al. ; Shiotani et al. ; Tanemura et al. ; Zuloaga et al. ) provided data on the DNT of DA following gestational exposure. See Tables 2 and 3 for brief summaries of study methods and outcomes.

For three rodent studies conducted by the subcutaneous (SC) route of exposure, the lowest LOAELs during gestation ranged between 0.6 to 1.5 mg/kg bw (Levin et al. ; Mills et al. ; Zuloaga et al. ). Reported outcomes included altered social behaviors and impaired maze performances.

A mouse gavage study administered DA daily on GD 10-17, at doses of 0, 1, or 3 mg DA/kg maternal bw-day (Shiotani et al. ). Postnatal behavioral testing of prenatally-exposed pups revealed both dose and sex influences on offspring performance. Significant changes were found in postweaning tests of motor coordination and indicators of anxiety behavior, with no identified NOAEL dose, while maternal animals showed no seizures or other effects at any tested dose.

A single IP injection of 1 mg DA/kg bw to pregnant mice was associated with behaviors indicating impaired learning and memory and increased anxiety in male offspring of 11 weeks postnatal age (Tanemura et al. ). The study also noted myelination failure and overgrowth of neuronal processes in limbic cortex neurons at necropsy of treated animals. In another study, a single IV dose of 0.6 mg DA/kg bw to pregnant dams altered postnatal electroencephalogram (EEG) results as well as histopathology and brain biochemistry (Dakshinamurti et al. ).
Zebrafish

Six studies used zebrafish as the test species for DA-induced DNT (Panlilio, Aluru, and Hahn ; Panlilio et al. ; Tiedeken and Ramsdell ; Tiedeken, Ramsdell, and Ramsdell ). Routes of exposure included "bath" exposure, microinjection, and IV injection. LOAELs by route were: 0.09E-6 mg DA/embryo by IV, 0.13E-6 mg/kg DA by microinjection, and 0.25 mM DA in the bath solution for larvae. Effects reported included seizures, reduced startle response, altered gene expression, reduced presence of reticulospinal neurons and primarily motor neuron axon collaterals, and disrupted myelination. See Table 4 for more details of study methods and findings.
Neonatal/Postnatal Exposure
Rodents

Young pups were dosed with DA in 18 rodent studies, and later assessed using behavioral and/or physiological studies at hours to weeks post-dosing. Only one study was conducted in mice, which was also the only study to use the gavage route (Sasaki et al. ). The other 17 studies used the rat model, with dosing by IP (Doucette et al. ; Xi, Peng, and Ramsdell ) and/or SC injection (Adams, Doucette, and Ryan ; Adams et al. ; Bernard et al. ; Burt, Ryan, and Doucette ; Doucette et al. ; Gill et al. ; Jandova et al. ; Levin et al. ; Marriott et al. ; Perry, Ryan, and Tasker ; Tasker et al. ; Thomsen et al. ; Wang et al. ). Twelve of the 18 studies used a 0.02 mg DA/kg bw-day dose on each of postnatal days (PND) 8-14. Once established as reliably resulting in DNT, in the absence of general offspring or maternal toxicity, this dosing protocol was used for all but one study published from 2005 through 2016. Dose and timing procedures were selected to ensure detectable DNT.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Studies varied in the evaluations performed and in age(s) at testing. Significant adverse effects included alterations in perceptual processing, altered social behavior and spontaneous activity patterns, increased stress-related behavior patterns and seizure activity, and altered maze performance with impaired responses to reversal challenges to previously learned mazes. Measurable effects were reported on open-field behaviors as late as PND 150 following dosing with 0.02 mg DA/kg-day on PND 8-14 (Burt, Ryan, and Doucette ). Tables 5 and 6 provide more details of methods and outcomes for these studies, including histopathology and biochemical results.
Wild California Sea Lions ( Zalophus californianus )

DA toxicosis has been identified and studied in stranded marine mammals, most extensively in the California sea lion. Four studies of young sea lions ranged in type from a case study of a single individual to observations of larger populations of, or including, immature animals (Goldstein et al. ; Krucik et al. ; Simeone et al. ).

These wild animals were exposed to DA in utero and/or via their mother's milk due to maternal consumption of a natural diet including DA-contaminated marine organisms. Older immature animals may also have been exposed by direct consumption of a DA-contaminated diet. Exact dosing is unknown, but exposure was inferred from the presence of Pseudo-nitzschia blooms of identified toxigenic size class and environmental monitoring in ocean waters near the sea lions' breeding and pupping locations (Smith et al. ). One study measured DA in bodily fluid samples from fetuses or pups (Goldstein et al. ). The others presumed DA-exposure based on documented environmental sampling and field observations, along with pathological symptoms specifically characteristic of DA toxicosis (Krucik et al. ; Simeone et al. ) and/or from identification of DA in tissues collected from other animals rescued at the same time and location (Goldstein et al. ).

Neurological effects were so profound as to cause death or preclude release of surviving animals back to the wild after post-stranding veterinary care. Effects included seizures (Goldstein et al. ; Simeone et al. ), adult-onset medial temporal lobe epilepsy (Krucik et al. ), brain edema (Goldstein et al. ), and hippocampal lesions including one animal with hippocampal-focused encephalitis (Simeone et al. ). See Table 7 for more information on study populations and observations.
Discussion

All the animal studies following gestational or larval exposure to DA (Tables 1, 2, 3, 4) reported DNT. While adverse effects were not detected at birth for prenatally-exposed monkeys (Burbacher et al. ), the same cohort of exposed infants demonstrated DNT at 1-2 months postnatal age (Grant et al. ). All but one study (Sasaki et al. ) of DA exposure in early postnatal life (Tables 5, 6, 7) reported DNT effects of DA. While different studies evaluated various specific effects, all of the observed outcomes are consistent with consequences of the known action of DA as an agonist of glutamate kainate receptors. Precise comparisons among studies for NOAEL and LOAEL doses are complicated by species-differences in DA TK parameters, which in turn influenced choices for experimental route of exposure. Most of the experimental animal studies were designed to investigate specific DNT outcomes, rather than to establish a dose-response relationship.
Gestational or Larval Experimental Exposures

The similarities between macaque monkeys and humans in TK models for oral DA exposure support experimental non-human primates as a particularly relevant model for gestational exposure linked to DNT (Jing et al. ; Shum et al. ). Data from other laboratory and wild species provide considerable supporting evidence for DNT following developmental exposure to similar dose levels of DA.

Impairment of recognition memory was found in 1-2 month-old  M. fascicularis  following repeated daily prenatal exposure to DA (Grant et al. ). The NOAEL from this study was 0.075 mg/kg bw-day, which is 10 times lower than the adult NOAEL of 0.75 mg/kg bw used to establish the TDI by the State of Washington (Marien ).

The prevalence of parenteral routes of exposure in the studies of gestational exposure to DA in laboratory rats and mice may reflect the findings of reduced DA absorption from the rodent gut as compared to humans and other primates (Iverson and Truelove ). Only one of five rodent injection studies administered a range of DA doses to pregnant rats (Levin et al. ). The study reported a NOAEL dose for DA of 0.3 mg/kg on GD 13, with a LOAEL of 0.6 mg/kg. Other investigators chose a single dose, selected to induce DNT outcomes in the absence of other observed toxic effects in offspring or maternal animals, and given to mice on a single gestation day (Dakshinamurti et al. ; Mills et al. ; Tanemura et al. ; Zuloaga et al. ). Results were generally consistent across these studies, even including the one oral mouse study (Shiotani et al. ), with LOAEL doses ranging from 0.6-1.5 mg/kg bw. Observed effects of DA included altered maze performance, locomotor impairments, reduced social behaviors, altered functional connectivity patterns and sensorimotor gating, effects on learning and anxiety behaviors, reduced seizure thresholds, and altered histopathology including myelination failure.

All but one zebrafish study was conducted by injection, either into a fertilized egg or embryo (Tiedeken and Ramsdell ; Tiedeken, Ramsdell, and Ramsdell ) or into a larval vein (Panlilio, Aluru, and Hahn ; Panlilio et al. ). While TK data for DA in zebrafish are not available, observations of excitotoxicity in adult anchovies given DA by intracoelomic injection suggested that fish may differ from mammals in distribution of absorbed DA, rather than in resistance to DA neurotoxicity (Lefebvre ). Zebrafish demonstrated similar symptoms and sensitivity to DA as other species studied (Panlilio, Aluru, and Hahn ; Tiedeken, Ramsdell, and Ramsdell ). (Panlilio, Aluru, and Hahn ) expressly chose test doses "similar to those causing behavioral effects in developing [neonatal] rodents," while also below levels "associated with acute toxicity in adult humans."

passages.text: Postnatal Experimental Exposures

Sasaki and colleagues administered a single oral dose of DA (3.0 mg/kg) to mice either on PND 14 or at 10 weeks postnatal age (adult), and conducted behavioral testing at 12-13 weeks postnatal age (Sasaki et al. ). In seeming contradiction to the generally greater sensitivity of immature individuals, effects on test performance were noted only in animals treated as adults. Treatment on PND 14, however, may have missed the critical window for irreversible developmental DA effects, while at the same time leaving 10 weeks for possible repair of transitory effects before testing at 12 weeks. The adult animals treated at 10 weeks had only two weeks recovery time before testing.

All of the early life experimental studies performed in rats used an injection method of DA exposure, with most giving repeated doses of 0 or 0.02 mg/kg-day on each of PNDs 8-14 (Adams, Doucette, and Ryan ; Adams et al. ; Bernard et al. ; Burt, Ryan, and Doucette ; Doucette et al. ; Gill et al. ; Marriott et al. ; Perry, Ryan, and Tasker ; Tasker et al. ; Thomsen et al. ). The lowest identified adverse effect dose for postnatal rat studies found seizure-like activity and altered hippocampal histopathology in adult animals following neonatal exposure to 0.005 mg/kg-day on PND 8-14 (Doucette et al. ).
Wild Sea Lions, Pre- and Post-Gestational Environmental Exposures

Wild California sea lions are large placental mammals, whose natural diet contains many of the same seafood species humans also enjoy eating. The Channel Islands off the coast of Santa Barbara, California, and surrounding waters are a primary breeding and pupping ground for these animals. Recurring Pseudo-nitzschia blooms have affected the area in recent decades, causing serious harm to sea lions as well as other wild species (Brodie et al. ; Goldstein et al. ).

A survey of pregnant female sea lions stranded during California's Pseudo-nitzschia blooms of 1998 and 2002 found 209 cases of reproductive failure attributed to DA exposure (Brodie et al. ). Types of reproductive failure included spontaneous abortion, premature live birth, fetal death, and maternal death prior to parturition. Another study specifically assessed DA contents in fetuses and fetal membranes from stranded pregnant females (Lefebvre et al. ). Although these studies did not assess DNT, they do provide context for evidence from surviving pups. In particular, the analysis of fetal body fluids demonstrated detectable levels of DA up to 8 days following maternal rescue (i.e., post cessation of environmental exposure).

Sea lion pups believed to have been exposed to DA, prenatally and/or neonatally, exhibited clinical symptoms and post-mortem brain pathology consistent with DA toxicosis (Goldstein et al. ; Krucik et al. ; Simeone et al. ). Beyond evidence that DA exposure occurred or was likely, quantitative exposure assessment for environmentally-exposed sea lions is not possible. Thus, direct comparisons cannot be made to adverse effect doses of DA identified for humans or experimental animal species. Additional complicating factors for assessment of sea lion data are the frequency of concurrent infections (e.g., bacterial, protozoal, viral), and contamination of the same habitat with chemicals such as DDTs and PCBs (Goldstein et al. ).
Life Course Considerations for Sensitivity to DA

The importance of a specific developmental stage to outcomes resulting from toxic exposures is a foundational principle of developmental toxicology (NRC ). The evidence summarized in this paper (Tables 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) supports a peak of susceptibility to DA during prenatal and/or early postnatal development, when developing vertebrate nervous tissues are most vulnerable.

Gestation and early infancy are not the only life stages with enhanced sensitivity to the neurological effects of DA. Exposures to DA late in life are also of elevated concern (Hendrix et al. ). An association between increased severity of effects and advanced age was noted in the initial sample of acutely poisoned adult humans (Perl, Bedard, Kosatsky, Hockin, Todd, Remis, et al. ; Wekell, Hurst, and Lefebvre ). All three patients who died in the hospital were over the age of 70, while only four of 19 hospitalized patients were under the age of 65. The younger hospitalized patients all had preexisting medical conditions, notably compromised kidney function. Experiments in mice compared sex and age for influence on sensitivity to effects of DA (Hendrix et al. ). Aged mice were found to be more susceptible to acute DA neurotoxicity than young adult mice, and females more sensitive than males. The older animals also accumulated higher concentrations of DA in serum and tissues compared to younger animals.

Concern has also been expressed for consequences of repeated, chronic exposures of healthy adult human populations to DA at levels below regulatory limits. A minimal, but detectable, memory decline was associated with repetitive sub-acute, dietary exposures to DA at levels below established allowable concentrations in the seafood consumed (Grattan et al. ; Stuchal et al. ). These effects were observed in a cohort of 500 adult Native American tribal members residing in coastal areas of the Pacific Northwest, who were studied over a period of 8 years, and who otherwise exhibited stable cognition.
Conclusions

For any toxin, adverse effect dose levels can vary with exposure patterns, the sensitivity of target tissues, as well as with TK factors such as rates of absorption and elimination. Apart from genetic variation within and between populations, life course considerations are critical for determining the sensitive windows for exposure to toxins (Halfon et al. ; Schaffer, Smith, and Faustman ).

Internationally, government agencies as well as individual researchers have opined that current regulatory standards for DA in seafood, which have not been revisited since initial implementation, may be insufficient to protect exposed individuals at all life stages and/or patterns of consumption (COT ; EFSA ; Grattan et al. ; Wekell, Hurst, and Lefebvre ).

Current US federal action levels for DA are based on a LOAEL of 1.0 mg DA/kg bw, adjusted by a 10-fold UF for within-species variation to a tolerable dose of 0.1 mg DA/ kg bw (DHHS ). The European Union adopted the Health Canada and US FDA regulatory limit of 20 ppm for DA in bivalve shellfish in 1997 (COT ; EU. ). The United Kingdom Food Standard Agency Committee on Toxicity (COT) (COT ), and the European Food Safety Authority Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (EFSA) (EFSA ), reviewed the regulatory limit for DA. Both groups considered an UF of 10 to be inadequate. The COT concluded that, while the action level "may protect against major outbreaks," it provides a "pragmatic guideline rather than a toxicologically based limit." EFSA noted that sensitive indicators of adverse neurological effects were not assessed in affected people during the 1987 ASP outbreak. EFSA recommended lowering the action limit to 4.5 ppm in shellfish meat, based on a 60 kg body weight, a 400 g meal size, and an additional UF of three to extrapolate from a LOAEL.

passages.text: In addition, or alternatively, to changing regulatory action levels, public health outreach to communities and groups at risk of DA-toxicity has been recommended (Grattan et al. ). Clinicians caring for patients sickened after consumption of seafood, particularly shellfish, could benefit from raised awareness of DA toxicity. Initial symptoms of general acute gastrointestinal illness combined with the rapid clearance of DA from the body may complicate accurate diagnosis (CPCS ). An example of relevant outreach is provided by the Washington State Department of Health, which issued an interim health advisory for regular consumers of razor clams containing allowable levels of DA recommending that consumers "...eat no more than 15 razor clams each month for 12 consecutive months...." (WADOH ). While the interim advisory is intended for everyone, sensitive subpopulations are specified: "...especially women who are or might become pregnant, nursing mothers, children, the elderly, and people with compromised renal function." Similar public health messaging on all potentially impacted types of seafood could be made more widely available through relevant agencies in affected states, and through educational materials for health professionals serving sensitive populations.
