passages.text: Dipeptides in CSF and plasma: diagnostic and therapeutic potential in neurological diseases

Dipeptides (DPs), composed of two amino acids (AAs), hold significant therapeutic potential but remain underexplored. Given the crucial role of AAs in central nervous system (CNS) function, this study investigated the presence of DPs in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and their correlation with corresponding AAs, potentially indicating their role as AA donors. Plasma and CSF samples were collected from 43 children with neurological or metabolic conditions of unknown origin, including 23 with epilepsy. A panel of 33 DPs was quantified using UPLC-MS/MS. Out of 33 DPs, 18 were detectable in CSF and 20 in plasma, displaying high inter-individual variance. Gly-Asp, Gly-Pro, and Ala-Glu were consistently found in all CSF samples, while only Gly-Asp was universally detectable in plasma. Anserine and carnosine were prominent in CSF and plasma, respectively, with no other histidine-containing DPs observed. Generally, DP concentrations were higher in plasma than in CSF; however, anserine and Gly-Pro had similar concentrations in both fluids. Significant correlations were observed between specific DPs and their corresponding AAs in CSF (Gly-Glu, Gly-Pro and Ser-Gln) and plasma (Glu-Glu and Glu-Ser). Notably, patients with epilepsy had elevated medium anserine concentrations in CSF. This study is the first to demonstrate the presence of numerous DPs in CSF and plasma. Further research is needed to determine if DP patterns can support the diagnosis of neurological diseases and whether DP administration can modulate amino acid availability in the brain, potentially offering new therapeutic options, such as for defects in the amino acid transporter.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00726-024-03434-1.
Introduction

Amino acids (AAs) are fundamental to numerous metabolic pathways within the brain and crucial for maintaining neurological functions, while the role of dipeptides (DPs) on neurological functions remains unclear. DPs, comprised of two AAs, are products of protein degradation with diverse biological effects beyond serving as amino acid donors, such as induction of anti-oxidative mechanisms (Saadati; Ozawa et al.; Aldini et al.), carbonyl sequestering activity (Aldini et al.; Weigand et al.), induction of H2S (Wetzel et al.), interaction with glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (Moreno et al.), exerts hydrolysis cleavage activity (Liu et al.) or improvement of endothelial sealing (Bartosova et al.). Further, non-proteinogenic amino acids have become a powerful tool for developing peptide-based drug candidates (Ding et al.).

Imbalances in AA metabolism, often caused by abnormalities in AA transporters, have been linked to neurological disorders, including epilepsy (Traynelis et al.; Lee; Malik and Willnow), schizophrenia (Adla et al.), autism spectrum disorders (Brister et al.) or Alzheimer's disease (Nuzzo et al.). Central to the pathophysiology is glutamate, the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which serves as a precursor for gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a key inhibitory neurotransmitter synthesized by l-glutamate decarboxylase (Bryson et al.; Albrecht et al.). The glutamate-glutamine cycle, a cyclical metabolic pathway, plays a pivotal role in maintaining a sufficient supply of the glutamate in the central nervous system. Notably, neurons cannot synthesize either glutamate or GABA directly from glucose. Furthermore, beyond the glutamate-glutamine axis, several other amino acids such as aspartate, glycine, GABA, tryptophan, histidine and tyrosine, pivotal for neurotransmission or as precursors to neurotransmitters, are essential for normal neurological function. Recent studies have shed light on alterations in the concentrations of various amino acids, including beta-alanine, glycine, serine, arginine, proline, methionine, cysteine and alanine in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with status epilepticus (Hanin). However, the role of DPs in the brain remains largely unclear. In patients with schizophrenia, not only a reduced concentration of glutamate but also of DP gamma-Glu-Gln was observed in the CSF (Do et al.). Even though it has been shown that the administration of carnosine plays a protective role in neurological diseases, it is still unclear to what extent oral administration of carnosine can influence CSF levels (Hegazy et al.).

The aim of this study is to investigate for the first time whether DPs are present in CSF and whether they can potentially serve as AA donors. In case of proteins that only occur in low concentrations in the CSF, increases are considered to be signs of inflammation, bleeding or other pathologies. Using ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (Heidenreich et al.), we attempt to identify DPs and AAs in epilepsy patient CSF and plasma collected simultaneously from patients. Because collecting CSF samples from healthy children is difficult, most CSF samples are from paediatric patients with neurological symptoms. This investigation holds promise for the discovery of new biomarkers and therapeutic targets in neurological disorders related to abnormalities in AA concentrations.
Materials and methods
Plasma and CSF samples

All patients have been admitted to Heidelberg University Hospital for further evaluation of unexplained neurological and/or metabolic conditions, including 23 patients with epilepsy or a history of seizures. Plasma and CSF was collected from patients taken at the same time. The children were aged between 2 weeks and 17 years (17 females and 26 males). Since the DP concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma are not very stable due to the presence of endogenous peptidases, all samples were immediately frozen after collecting and stored at - 80 C. Epilepsy was classified into "epilepsy yes or no" and "focal" or "generalized". All samples were acquired between January and March 2023. This study was approved by the ethic committee of the University Heidelberg (S-554/2018).
Dipeptide and amino acid quantification

33 DP were determined by an UPLC-MS/MS method as described by Heidenreich (Heidenreich, et al.). Alanyl-Alanine (Ala-Ala), Alanyl-Glutamine (Ala-Gln), Alanyl-Glutamate (Ala-Glu), Alanyl-Glycine (Ala-Gly), Alanyl-Histidine (Ala-His), Alanyl-Phenylalanine (Ala-Phe), Alanyl-Proline (Ala-Pro), Alanyl-Tyrosine (Ala-Tyr), Anserine, Aspartyl-Glutamine (Asp-Gln), Carnosine, Glutamyl-Glutamate (Glu-Glu), gamma-Glutamyl-epsilon-Lysine (gamma-Glu-epsilon-Lys), Glutamyl-Serine (Glu-Ser), Glycyl-Aspartate (Gly-Asp), Glycyl-Glutamate (Gly-Glu), Glycyl-Histidine (Gly-His), Glycyl-Phenylalanine (Gly-Phe), Glycyl-Proline (Gly-Pro), Histidyl-Alanine (His-Ala), Histidyl-Leucine (His-Leu), Histidyl-Serine (His-Ser), Leucyl-Histidine (Leu-His), Leucyl-Proline (Leu-Pro), Phenylalanyl-Alanine (Phe-Ala), Prolyl-Glycine (Pro-Gly), Prolyl-Leucine (Pro-Leu), Seryl-Alanine (Ser-Ala), Seryl-Glutamine (Ser-Gln), Seryl-Histidine (Ser-His), Tyrosyl-Alanine (Tyr-Ala), Tyrosyl-Phenylalanine (Tyr-Phe), Valyl-Tyrosine (Val-Tyr) were measured via UPLC-MS/MS. A panel of 18 amino acids were determined as previously described by Weger et al. including alanine (Ala), arginine (Arg), asparagine (Asn), aspartate (Asp), glutamine (Gln), glutamate (Glu), glycine (Gly), histidine (His), isoleucine (Ile), leucine (Leu), lysine (Lys), methionine (Met), phenylalanine (Phe), proline (Pro), serine (Ser), threonine (Thr), tyrosine (Tyr) and valine (Val).
Method validation

The method has been established and validated as described previously (Heidenreich et al.). In brief, each DP is represented by a specific multiple reaction monitoring with the fragment mass 171.1, derived from the AccQ-Tag  reagent. A second qualifying fragment (Q3) was included where possible. MS/MS parameters were optimized for all derivatized DPs via manual tuning and flow-injection analysis. Baseline separation was achieved for isomeric DPs. Ala-Leu and Leu-Ala shared the same retention time and could not be discriminated. Cys-Gly had a high background peak, affecting quantification. Gly-Leu and Leu-Gly separated well but showed a strong background peak, complicating quantification at lower concentrations. Signal intensity and calibration range vary between DPs. The limit of quantification ranged from 0.1 to 2.5 fmol depending on the analyte. DPss with multiple amine groups, like His-containing DPs, generally showed lower signal intensities compared to those with a single amine group.
Statistical analysis

Results in figures are presented as mean +- SD unless stated otherwise. Correlations were calculated using Spearman correlation coefficient via Graph Pad Prism. Mann-Whitney test and Area-under-the-curve analysis were used for determination of a statistically significant difference between two groups via Graph Pad Prism. Age- and gender-specific effects have been evaluated by multiple linear regression analysis.
Results
Dipeptide distribution in plasma and CSF

Out of the 33 DPs investigated, 18 were detectable in CSF and 20 in plasma, with Gly-Asp, Gly-Pro and Ala-Glu present in all 43 CSF samples, and only Gly-Asp in all plasma samples. Ala-Pro, Ala-Gly, Ala-Phe were only detectable in plasma but not in CSF, Leu-Pro was only detectable in CSF and not in plasma. DPs that could not be determined due to low detection (below baseline), due to a very poor signal-to-noise ratio or strong overlap with an unknown co-eluting peak have not been considered in the calculations.

Dipeptide concentrations (fmol/microl) in CSF (A) and plasma (B) of 43 CSF samples from children with neurological or metabolic conditions of unknown origin. In CSF, out of 43 patients, anserine was detectably in 24 patients, Gly-Asp in 43, Carnosine in 4, gamma-Glu-epsilon-Lys in 36, Asp-Gln in 26, Gly-Pro in 43, Glu-Ser in 21, Ser-Gln in 17, Ala-Glu in 43, Pro-Gly in 42, Gly-Glu in 23, Ala-Ala in 24, Ser-Ala in 13, Glu-Glu in 21, Gly-Phe in 3, Val-Tyr in 22, Phe-Ala in 3 and Leu-Pro in 13. In plasma, anserine was detectably in 12 patients, Gly-Asp in 43, Carnosine in 12, gamma-Glu-epsilon-Lys in 3, Asp-Gln in 14, Gly-Pro in 42, Glu-Ser in 25, Ser-Gln in 17, Ala-Glu in 42, Pro-Gly in 39, Gly-Glu in 37, Ala-Ala in 28, Ser-Ala in 23, Glu-Glu in 37, Gly-Phe in 9, Val-Tyr in 21, Phe-Ala in 15, Ala-Gly in 27, Ala-Pro in 24 and Ala-Phe in 1. Displayed is a Tukey-Box-Plot

The histidine-containing DP anserine was the highest occurring DP in the CSF, followed by Gly-Asp, carnosine and gamma-Glu-epsilon-Lys. In plasma, carnosine was the DP with the highest mean concentration, albeit only in 12 of 43 plasma samples detectable, followed by anserine (Fig. 1). None of the other histidine-containing DPs measured were detectable in plasma and CSF (Ala-His, His-Ala, His-Leu, His-Ser, Leu-His, Ser-His). Since Glu and Gln play a central role in neurotransmission in brain, we investigated how many of the DPs contain these two amino acids. All 4 investigated Glu-containing DPs (Glu-Ser, Ala-Glu, Gly-Glu, Glu-Glu) were detectable and 2 (Asp-Gln and Ser-Gln) out of 3 Gln-containing DPs were detectable in the CSF samples, Ala-Gln was below detection limit. Other DPs containing AAs involved in neurotransmitters, such as aspartate or glycine, were also present in the CSF (Asp-Gln, Gly-Asp, Gly-Pro, Pro-Gly, Gly-Glu, Gly-Phe). The multiple linear regression analysis did not reveal any gender- or age-specific distribution patterns for the DPs in CSF and plasma, with the exception of anserine in CSF, which was found to be reduced in patients under 10 years of age (p < 0.03). However, due to the limited sample size, particularly among patients older than 10 years,drawing definitive conclusions is challenging.

To understand the relationship between plasma and CSF DP profile, we determined the relation of DP and AA concentrations between plasma and CSF. 17 of the DPs and 18 AAs were detectable in both, CSF and plasma (Table 2, Suppl. Table 2). While the concentrations of some DPs in CSF and plasma were in a similar concentration range, such as anserine or Gly-Pro, the concentration of other DPs, such as Ser-Ala or Gly-Phe, was many times lower in CSF than in plasma. Even though the concentration of Pro-Gly and Gly-Pro in plasma were in a similar range, the concentration of Pro-Gly in CSF was much lower than that of its stereoisomer. The concentrations of proline and glutamate were much lower in CSF than in plasma (Suppl. Table 2). A significant correlation between CSF and plasma DP concentrations was found for Ala-Ala (r > 0.78; p < 0.01; Suppl Table 3).
Dipeptide levels in CSF of children with and without epilepsy: a comparative study

The concentrations of the three DPs present in all patients, Gly-Asp (A), Gly-Pro (B) and Ala-Glu (C) and anserine (D), the DP with the highest concentration on average in CSF of patients without (w/o) and with epilepsy (in fmol/microl). Anserine was detectable in 12 patients without and with epilepsy, Gly-Asp, Gly-Pro and Ala-Glu in 20 patients without and in 23 patients with epilepsy. The mean values of these DPs tend to be higher for patients with epilepsy than for patients without epilepsy, but did only reach statistical significance in anserine. Mann-Whitney test was used for statistical evaluation. Displayed is mean +- SD. *p < 0.05. ns = not significant

We compared DP/AA concentrations in children with and without epilepsy. Out of the 23 patients with epilepsy, 4 had focal seizure, while 10 were classified as having generalized epilepsy. For 9 patients, information on the type of seizure was missing. Three of the patients received valproate (VPA), one with focal and one with generalized epilepsy (Suppl. Table 4). There was no obvious difference in DP and AA pattern in CSF of the patients receiving valproate. The DP concentrations varied greatly between patients. The mean concentrations of the three DPs that were detectable in all CSF samples (Gly-Asp, Gly-Pro, Ala-Glu) tend to be higher in patients with epilepsy than in patients without epilepsy, but without reaching statistical significance (Fig. 2). Anserine, the DP present at the highest average concentration, was found to be 1.8 times higher in patients with epilepsy compared to those without epilepsy (p < 0.05). However, this difference may be influenced by age, as the epilepsy group was, on average, younger than the non-epilepsy group (3 years vs. 7 years, respectively). This observation was further supported by area-under-the-curve (AUC) analysis, which showed the following AUC values for Gly-Asp, Gly-Pro, and Ala-Glu: 0.504, 0.554, and 0.555, respectively (Confidence Intervals: 0.35-0.68, 0.77-0.73, and 0.37-0.72, p = n.s.). In contrast, only for anserine the AUC was significantly higher (AUC: 0.75; Confidence Interval: 0.55-0.95; p < 0.037). There was no detectable difference in DPs between the small sub-cohorts of patients with generalized and focal seizures in CSF and plasma (Suppl. Table 5 A-D).
Discussion

Dipeptides (DPs) represent a class of compounds that have received limited attention in scientific research and human biology until now. DPs can originate from both dietary intake and internal protein breakdown, with the potential for 400 different DPs to emerge from the 20 proteinogenic Amino acids (AAs). Recent investigations have unveiled a significant presence of DPs across various organs, urine, and serum of mice (Heidenreich et al.), as well as in the human kidney (Pfeffer et al.). Beyond serving as AA donors they have diverse biological effects such as induction of anti-oxidative mechanisms (Saadati; Ozawa et al.; Aldini et al.), carbonyl sequestering activity (Aldini et al.; Weigand et al.), induction of H2S (Wetzel et al.), interaction with glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (Moreno et al.) or improvement of endothelial sealing (Bartosova et al.). Notably, DPs exhibit distinct distribution patterns among organs in mice, hinting at an organ-specific metabolic regulation within the body. Recognizing the pivotal role of AAs in neurological functions, we aimed to explore the presence of DPs in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), their correlation with corresponding AAs and the potential relationship between plasma and CSF DP profiles.

We demonstrate the presence of numerous DPs in both CSF and plasma in humans, albeit at relatively low concentrations. The DP concentration in CSF and plasma was significantly lower than that of the AAs, but if one considers the sum of all 400 DPs, the concentrations of all DPs are presumably in a similar concentration range as their corresponding AAs. In particular, the inter-individual differences in DP concentrations were considerable, as only certain DPs were detected in all patients. Among the detected DPs, anserine emerged with notably higher concentrations than carnosine and other DPs, while other histidine-containing DPs, apart from anserine and carnosine, were absent. The presence of carnosine and anserine in the brain has already been demonstrated in humans (Boldyrev et al.). Anserine is formed by the methylation of carnosine (Kwiatkowski et al.) and both DPs are degraded by the Carnosinase 1 (CN1), an enzyme which very specifically degrades only histidine-containing DPs, also present in the brain (Teufel et al.). A disorder of carnosinase 1, carnosinemia or homocarnosinemia, has been described, but a connection between the enzyme and the phenotype has never been shown (Sjaastad et al.; Peters et al.; Pfeffer et al.). In contrast, numerous therapeutic approaches are being investigated for these DPs (Caruso et al.), e.g. in the context of cognitive functions and their decline (Caruso et al.; Masuoka et al.), neurodegenerative diseases (Solana-Manrique et al.), cancer (Maugeri et al.), late complications of diabetes (Matthews et al.; Peters et al.) in humans or in an epilepsy rat model (Qi et al.). Furthermore, Gly-Asp was detectable at relatively high levels, consistent with its prevalence in various mouse organs, including the brain (Heidenreich et al.). Gly-Asp cannot be degraded by CN1 or CN2 (Pfeffer et al.). It is an anionic DP with a high resistance to hydrolysis compared to DPs with bulky residues in the N-terminal position (Rohm et al.). Additionally, DPs containing Glu, Gln, Asp, and Gly residues were prominently present in the CSF of the patients.

In line with previous studies (Akiyama et al.), the AA concentrations were higher in plasma than in CSF, especially for proline and glutamate. While the concentrations for some DPs were in the same range in plasma and CSF, e.g. for anserine or Gly-Pro, the concentrations of Ser-Ala and Gly-Phe in CSF were many times lower than in plasma. The plasma/CSF ratio for AAs is considered as an indicator of AA transport with several transporters described (Zaragoza). Cellular uptake of DPs occurs by proton-coupled oligopeptide transporters (POTs) via an inwardly-directed proton gradient and negative membrane potential. At present, four members of the POT family, namely PEPT1 (SLC15A1), PEPT2 (SLC15A2), PHT1 (SLC15A4) and PHT2 (SLC15A3), have been identified in mammals (Jappar et al.). In the brain, PEPT2 in particular seems to play an important role contributing to the peptide homeostasis (Smith et al.). To date, the transport of DPs has primarily been investigated during intestinal absorption and little is known about transport across the blood-brain barrier. The intestinal uptake of DPs and their distribution in the blood depends very much on the DP structure (Rohm et al.). However, in a previous study the DPs glycyl-glutamine and glycyl-tyrosine were administered to healthy individuals and their concentrations were quantified in blood and CSF. However, the administration of these DPs did not increased their concentration in the CSF (Himmelseher et al.). Whether other DP can pass the blood-brain barrier may depend on their structure and needs further studies. These DPs could be of therapeutic use, both in their function as AA donors and in their properties that go beyond those of the individual AAs. The correlation of DPs between plasma and CSF is an important parameter to better understand an indication of a possible transport of the DP into the CSF. Although the correlations between plasma and CSF concentrations were rather low in our cohort, a correlation for some of the DPs was detected, especially alanine and glycine-containing DPs. Considering the role of DPs as AA donors, we tested the correlation between DPs and their corresponding AAs. In CSF, our cohort shows for several DPs a correlation with their corresponding AAs. However, DPs are not the only source of AAs. Additionally, previous findings from DP and AA profiles in different tissues of mice suggest the influence of metabolic activity on their relation (Heidenreich et al.). Even though the influence of valproate on AA concentrations in the brain has been proven (Wislowska-Stanek et al.; Anderson et al.), we could not find a clear influence of valproate on the DP and AA pattern in our cohort. Studies in larger cohorts would be necessary for a clear statement.

The present study shows for the first time the presence of many DPs in blood and CSF. This study is a preliminary study with some limitations. Although there was a trend that DP concentrations in epileptic children were generally higher as for non-epileptic children but this trend reached significant differences only for anserine, which might be caused by age-dependent effects. However, there were no clear indications of sex- or age-dependent variability of the DPs, except anserine, in plasma and CSF, but more samples are needed for definitive conclusions. The DP concentration also shows a high intra-individual range, so this trend should be viewed with caution. As it is generally difficult to obtain plasma and CSF samples from children, the group size of 43 patients is limiting for statistical conclusions. In addition, we only used samples from which plasma and CSF samples were taken simultaneously. Since healthy children do not undergo CSF and plasma sampling, the controls are also children with unexplained neurological symptoms. This is another factor that makes it difficult to compare the patient groups. The influence of food on DP concentrations was also not considered in this study. Even if the concentrations of AAs and DPs in the serum are strongly dependent on the diet and certainly explain part of the strong inter-individual differences, the ratio of DPs in serum and CSF is certainly only minimally influenced by this. Additionally, the DPs and AAs are components of a continuous metabolic process. The measurements can, of course, only provide a snapshot of this process. Despite these limitations, this study reveals new, previously undescribed findings on DPs and their corresponding AAs and will hopefully stimulate further investigations.

In conclusion, this study is the first to identify the presence of numerous DPs in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Measuring DP concentrations can indicate pathological changes. For example, we found that mean anserine concentrations, the DP with the highest concentration in CSF, are elevated in patients with epilepsy. Since several detected DPs in CSF correlate with their respective AAs and some with their plasma concentrations, therapeutic concepts involving the administration of DPs for neurological diseases with altered AA levels are conceivable. While therapeutic approaches targeting DPs are being explored for various diseases, further research is needed to clarify their exact functions and effects on neurological conditions.

passages.text: Conformational switching of Arp5 subunit regulates INO80 chromatin remodeling
Abstract

The INO80 chromatin remodeler is a versatile enzyme capable of several functions, including spacing nucleosomes equal distances apart, precise positioning of nucleosomes based on DNA shape/sequence and exchanging histone dimers. Within INO80, the Arp5 subunit plays a central role in INO80 remodeling, evidenced by its interactions with the histone octamer, nucleosomal and extranucleosomal DNA, and its necessity in linking INO80's ATPase activity to nucleosome movement. We find two distinct regions of Arp5 binding near the acidic pocket of nucleosomes. One region has an arginine anchor that binds nucleosomes and is vital for INO80 mobilizing nucleosomes. The other region has a hydrophobic/acid patch of Leu and Asp that binds free histone H2A-H2B dimers. These two regions have different roles in remodeling nucleosomes as seen both in vitro and in vivo and the hydrophobic/acidic patch of Arp5 is likely needed for displacing DNA from the H2A-H2B surface and dimer exchange by INO80.
Graphical Abstract
Introduction

The holocomplex referred to as INO80, with its catalytic subunit known as Ino80, plays a pivotal role in chromatin remodeling and is important in transcription regulation, DNA repair and replication, nuclear organization and cellular differentiation. INO80 remodels chromatin by repositioning nucleosomes in a DNA shape and sequence-dependent manner, placing nucleosomes equally separated by the same length of linker DNA and facilitating the exchange of histone dimers. Deletion of Ino80 hampers ventricular compaction during heart development and correlates with defective coronary vascularization. Mutations in YY1AP1, a subunit of INO80, disrupt smooth muscle differentiation and are associated with Grange syndrome that occasionally manifests as arterial disease. Elevated expression of Ino80 is crucial for the proliferation of melanoma, small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and colon cancer. INO80 increases accessibility at enhancer regions in melanoma and SCLC, thereby facilitating Mediator complex binding. Additionally, at centromeres INO80 displaces canonical H3 to promote the incorporation of CENP-A and is required for the ectopic incorporation of CENP-A when overexpressed. In homologous recombination, INO80 facilitates Rad21 filament formation and DNA re-sectioning through the removal of H2A.Z. H2A.Z removal by INO80 also occurs at pericentric regions and certain promoters, although at many promoters RNA polymerase II primarily displaces H2A.Z.

passages.text: One of the distinctive architectural features of INO80 is the binding of the Arp8 module to linker DNA, which is tethered to the Ino80 catalytic subunit via the HSA (helicase-SANT-associated) domain of Ino80. This binding is disrupted by either truncating the N-terminus of Arp8 or by mutating the DNA binding surface of the HSA domain. The nucleosome mobilizing activity of INO80 is significantly impaired when the Arp8 module fails to bind linker DNA, suggesting that this mechanism governs INO80's nucleosome spacing and potentially enables the positioning of nucleosomes in a DNA shape-specific manner.

Another architectural element of INO80 is the Arp5 module that interacts with the histone octamer, nucleosomal DNA at SHL-1, -2 and -3 and extranucleosomal DNA where DNA enters nucleosomes. Arp5 forms a heterodimer with the Ies6 subunit in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Sc) and contains a flexible grappler domain that exhibits two alternative conformations known as the 'cross' and 'parallel' conformations, as observed by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Recently, an improved structure of Chaetomium thermophilum (Ct) INO80:NCP and AlphaFold2 modeling of the grappler domain has provided insights into the 'cross' conformation of the grappler domain. In this model, regions termed the 'foot' and 'heel' bind to the acidic pocket of nucleosomes using an arginine anchor. This model is supported by mutations in the arginine anchor and other regions of Arp5 predicted to interact with nucleosomal DNA effectively blocking nucleosome mobilization by Ct INO80.

The acidic pocket represents a crucial binding site on the nucleosome, characterized by a negatively charged depression. It serves as a binding site for various chromatin-associated factors, including viral proteins, histone modifiers and ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers. Interactions at this site play pivotal roles in regulating transcription, DNA repair and other genomic processes.

In this study, we confirm the presence of a weak arginine anchor in the grappler domain of Sc Arp5 which binds to the acidic pocket and is required for the nucleosome mobilizing activity of INO80. Somewhat surprisingly, we find there is another part of Arp5 that also binds to the lateral face of the nucleosome distinct from the arginine anchor based on different INO80 phenotypes and biochemical properties. This other region has a high affinity for free H2A-H2B dimers, does not appear to bind directly to the acidic pocket and based on structural models is spatially disparate from the arginine anchor. We provide evidence for the grappler domain dynamically switching contact with the nucleosome that is likely important for the dimer exchange activity of INO80.
Materials and methods
Yeast strains, plasmids and Anchor Away system

Strains used in this study are W303 (MATa his3-11, 15 leu2-3 112 trp1Delta ura3-1 ade2-1 can1-100) or BY4741 (MATalpha his3Delta1 leu2Delta0 met15Delta0) or their derivatives (Supplementary Table S1). Sc BY4741 (MATalpha his3Delta1 leu2Delta0 met15Delta0) strain with a 2 - FLAG (DYKDDDDK) tag epitope attached at the C-terminus of the Ino80 subunit was used for wild-type (WT) INO80 complex purification. DeltaArp5 strain [BY4741 (MATalpha his3Delta1 leu2Delta0 met15Delta0 ura3Delta0 Arp5Delta::KanMX INO80-2XFLAG::Leu2)] was used to purify the Arp5 mutant complexes. For Arp5 hemagglutinin epitope tag (HA) tagged or mutant complexes (Arp5DBD, Arp5LLD, Arp Delta516-564), Sc Arp5 ORF with corresponding residue mutations was cloned into pRS-416 plasmid along with flanking 935 bp upstream and 932 bp downstream regions containing its endogenous promoter and terminator (for Arp5R3 mutant, the flanking upstream and downstream regions were reduced to 638 bp and +268 bp of Arp5 ORF, respectively). The plasmids containing the mutations were then transformed into the Arp5 deletion strain (Arp5Delta) and purified using by immunoaffinity chromatography.

An Anchor Away (AA) system was employed for the phenotypic characterization of Arp5 mutations. Briefly, Sc W303 (CY1827) (MATa tor1-1 fpr1::loxP-LEU2-loxP RPL13A-2 x FKBP12::loxP bar1Delta::HISG) or WT-S288C-AA (MATalpha tor1-1 fpr1Delta RPL13A-FKBP12::NAT his3Delta leu2Delta lys2Delta ura3Delta) strain was used to create Arp5 AA strain (Arp5-FRB-W303 or Arp5-FRB-S288C). Endogenous Arp5 was tagged with the FRB domain at the C-terminus using a cassette containing FRB domain and G418 selection marker which was amplified from pFA6a-FRB-KanMX6 plasmid (Supplementary Table S1) using the primer ARP5_C_F1 and ARP5_C_R1. The tagged transformants were selected using G418 selection marker and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction. The Arp5-FRB strain was then transformed with various pRS-416 Arp5 mutant plasmids using a standard lithium acetate yeast transformation protocol. The Arp5-FRB-W303 strains for the phenotypic screenings and characterization were transformed with the pRS416 and Arp5 mutant plasmids containing ~638 bp upstream and ~268 bp downstream of Arp5 ORF flanking region.
Purification of INO80 complexes

Native Sc WT and mutant Arp5 complexes were purified using immunoaffinity purification with 2 - FLAG (DYKDDDDK) epitopes attached at the C-terminus of the catalytic subunit Ino80. Yeast strains (Supplementary Table S1) were grown in 100 ml YPD culture (1% yeast extract, 2% peptone, 2% dextrose, 40 ppm antifoam A and 0.05% adenine sulfate) for WT Arp5 or in synthetic complete media -Ura for mutant Arp5-containing complexes. The 100 ml cultures were added to 15 l YPD culture (1% yeast extract, 2% peptone, 2% dextrose, 40 ppm antifoam A and 0.05% adenine sulfate) and incubated with stirring until the OD600 reached 5-6. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 4 C, washed with sterile water and H-0.3 buffer [300 mM NaCl, 25 mM Na-HEPES pH 7.8, 0.5 mM ethylene glycol tetraacetic acid (EGTA), 0.1 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), 2 mM MgCl2, 20% glycerol and 0.02% NP-40] plus protease inhibitors (1 mM phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), 1 mM beta-mercaptoethanol, 0.5 Na-metabisulphite, 2 muM pepstatin, 0.6 muM leupeptin, 2 mM benzamidine and 2 mug/ml chymostatin). Yeast spaghetti was prepared from pellets by extrusion into liquid nitrogen and cryogenically ground using a Spex freezer miller 6870. The yeast powder was re-suspended with H-0.3 buffer plus inhibitors, and the nuclear proteins were extracted by ultracentrifugation at 100 000 x g for 1 h. The supernatant was incubated overnight at 4 C with Anti-FLAG M2 agarose beads (Sigma-Aldrich) (10 mul beads per ml extract) in buffer H-0.3 with protease inhibitors. The resin was washed several times with H-0.5 buffer followed by H-0.1 buffer (same composition as H-0.3 buffer but containing 500 mM and 100 mM of NaCl, respectively) with protease inhibitors. FLAG-tagged protein complexes were eluted with a 1 mg/ml solution of 3X-FLAG peptide in buffer H-0.1 + 1mM PMSF. The integrity and quantification of the purified complexes were examined by 4-20% sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and SYPRO Ruby staining.
Western blots

Purified INO80 with WT Arp5 and Arp5 tagged with HA are resolved on a 20 cm x 20 cm 4-20% Tris-glycine-SDS polyacrylamide gels and transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes using Bio-Rad Trans-Blot  electrophoretic transfer cell for 3 h at 4 C, using a transfer buffer containing 25 mM Tris, 192 mM glycine, 20% methanol and 0.1% SDS (pH 8.3) at 50 V constant voltage. The membranes were blocked with 5% fat-free milk in Tris-Buffered Saline with Tween 20 (TBST) (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween-20), overnight at 4 C, washed with TBST and incubated with anti-HA antibody (Supplementary Table S1) diluted as 1:1000 for 1 h at room temperature. The blots were washed with TBST and developed with SuperSignal  West Femto Maximum Sensitivity Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) before visualization using an Image Quant LAS 4000 (GE Healthcare Life Sciences).
Phenotypic screening

WT and mutant Arp5 cells were grown overnight in 5 ml synthetic complete -Ura media at 30 C. The overgrown cell cultures were diluted back to ~OD600 nm of 0.3 in YPD medium and were allowed to grow till they reached ~OD600 nm of 0.7. Further, 5-fold serial dilutions were made for each culture and the original culture (at OD600 ~1) as well as the serial dilutions were stamped using a pin-frogger onto -Ura, Hydroxyurea (HU), 6-azauracil (6-AU) or methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) plates, in presence or absence of rapamycin (final concentrations used have been mentioned in the figure legends). Samples were allowed to dry and plates were then turned over and incubated at 30 C for (37 C for heat shock treatment experiments) for 2-3 d or until the appearance of yeast colonies.
Histone crosslinking

Recombinant Xenopus laevis histones with amino acids replaced by cysteine at specific positions (Supplementary Figure S1A) were expressed, purified and reconstituted into octamers with other histones as discussed above. Homogeneous 70N5 WT nucleosomes were reconstituted using the respective 601-nucleosome positioning sequence. The modified nucleosomes were then conjugated with PEAS [N-((2-pyridyldithio)ethyl)-4-azidosalicylamide] (Thermo Fisher Scientific), iodinated with [125I] and bound to saturating concentrations of WT or mutant Arp5 complexes. Samples were crosslinked by ultraviolet (UV) irradiation for 3 min at 310 nm, 2.65 mW/cm2. After crosslinking, the [125I]-radiolabel was transferred to the crosslinked proteins by incubating with 100 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) for 30 min at 37 C. Proteins were separated on 4-20% SDS polyacrylamide gels, dried and viewed by phosphorimaging.
Peptide mapping of Ino80 subunit with ArgC protease

After label transfer, photoaffinity-labeled Arp5 complexes were denatured with 0.4% SDS and heated at 90 C for 3 min, followed by buffer exchange using Amicon Ultra filters to remove SDS and HA peptides. The C-terminal HA-tagged Arp5 was immobilized using anti-HA beads, equilibrated in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.8), 5 mM CaCl2 and 2 mM EDTA and cleavage initiated by the addition of DTT (5 mM final concentration) and varying concentrations of ArgC protease (Promega, sequencing grade). Reactions were incubated at 37 C for 2 h and stopped by the addition of 1 mM PMSF and 10 mM EDTA. The proteolytic fragments not immobilized to the beads were removed by washing 3 times with the same buffer as the digestion. The bead fractions were denatured in SDS sample buffer and resolved on 4-20% Tris-glycine-SDS polyacrylamide gels, which are further processed by phosphorimaging and anti-HA immunoblotting. Apparent molecular masses of the Arp5-HA fragments were estimated by comparing their migration relative to the [35S]-labeled Arp5-HA described before.
Binding assay

Cy5 labeled DNA template was amplified for 70N5 601 DNA templates and nucleosomes were reconstituted. An increasing concentration of INO80 complex (WT or mutant) was incubated with 25 nM nucleosome at 30 C for 30 min, in 10 mM Na-HEPES (pH 7.8), 4 mM MgCl2, 60 mM NaCl, 0.2 mM EGTA, 0.04 mM EDTA and 8% glycerol. Reactions were analyzed by resolving enzyme-bound nucleosomes from free nucleosomes on 4% native polyacrylamide gels in 1x Tris-EDTA buffer. Data images in the figures are representative of n = 3 experiments.
Nucleosome reconstitution and remodeling

Initially 5' end of the forward primer for 70N5 601 DNA template was labeled with 50 muCi of [32P]-ATP using T4 phosphokinase. Then [32P]-labeled primer and unlabeled reverse primer were used to amplify the 70N5 601 template DNA. Mononucleosomes were reconstituted with 1.7 mug of 5mg/ml salmon sperm DNA and 100 fmol of [32P]-labeled 70N5 601 DNA at 37 C with 3-5 mug of recombinant X. laevis histone octamers by rapid salt-dilution from 2 M to 280 mM NaCl in 10-min steps. The reconstitution was evaluated by native 4% polyacrylamide gel (35.36 acrylamide: 1 bisacrylamide) electrophoresis, followed by phosphorimaging (Typhoon FLA 9500 laser scanner, GE Healthcare Life Sciences). In the case of nucleosome remodeling, the reconstituted nucleosomes (24 nM) were incubated with saturating amounts of INO80 complexes (25 nM) at 30 C for 30 min. Nucleosome sliding was initiated by adding ATP to a final concentration of 80 muM, and remodeling reactions were stopped at the indicated time points by adding 2 mmol of EDTA and 1 mug of salmon sperm DNA (stop mix). Samples were analyzed on 5% native polyacrylamide gels in 0.5x Tris/Borate/EDTA (TBE) buffer and phosphorimaged as before.
ATPase assay

ATPase assays were performed under conditions identical to the remodeling time course assays. After pre-binding, initially a premix of ATP was prepared containing 1 mM of cold ATP supplemented with 0.5 mul of 3000 Ci/mmol gamma-32P-labeled ATP. ATP mix was added to nucleosome bound complex such that the final concentration of cold ATP was 80muM. Reactions were allowed to proceed for the indicated timepoints. Reactions were stopped by addition of EDTA and SDS to final concentrations of 100 mM and 2%, respectively. Reactions were spotted onto a polyethyleneimine cellulose plate (J.T. Baker) and developed with 0.5 M LiCl and 0.5 M formic acid.
Histone crosslinking

Recombinant X. laevis histones with amino acids replaced by cysteine at specific positions (Supplementary Figure S1A) were expressed, purified and reconstituted into octamers with other histones as discussed above. Homogeneous 70N5 WT nucleosomes were reconstituted using the respective 601-nucleosome positioning sequence. The modified nucleosomes were then conjugated with PEAS [N-((2-pyridyldithio)ethyl)-4-azidosalicylamide] (Thermo Fisher Scientific), iodinated with [125I] and bound to saturating concentrations of WT or mutant Arp5 complexes. Samples were crosslinked by UV irradiation for 3 min at 310 nm, 2.65 mW/cm2. After crosslinking, the [125I]-radiolabel was transferred to the crosslinked proteins by incubating with 100 mM DTT for 30 min at 37 C. Proteins were separated on 4-20% SDS polyacrylamide gels, dried and viewed by phosphorimaging.
Peptide pulldown

Biotin-labeled peptides (Supplementary Table S1) were obtained from SYN high-quality peptide (Shanghai, China). Streptavidin beads (25 mul) were washed in buffer containing 1x phosphate buffered saline (PBS) pH 7.4 and 0.01% bovine serum albumin (BSA) and incubated with 10 mug of biotin-labeled peptide for 30 min at room temperature with gentle rotation, followed by magnetic pulldown for 2-3 min. The supernatant was discarded, and the coated beads were washed 4 times with PBS containing 0.1% BSA and re-suspended at 25 mul final volume. Coated beads were incubated with 5 mug nucleosome containing 5' [32P]-labeled DNA or H2A/B dimer in 500 mul binding buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris-HCl, 10% Glycerol and 0.1% NP-40) overnight at 4 C with gentle rotation. Next, beads were washed 4 times with 1 ml binding buffer, followed by the addition of 25 mul of 1x Laemmilli buffer and boiling for 5 min. Samples were analyzed by 17% SDS-PAGE, histones were visualized by using SYPRO Ruby gel stain (Cat#S12000; Invitrogen) and corresponding radiolabeled DNA was visualized by phosphorimaging.
Peptide competition experiments

WT and mutant LLD peptides were incubated at varied concentrations with reconstituted 601 nucleosomes for 20 minutes at 30 C. INO80 was added to nucleosomes pre-incubated with peptides for 30 min at the same temperature and remodeling initiated by the addition of ATP to a final concentration of 80 muM. After 10 min, reaction was stopped as described previously and resolved on a 5% native polyacrylamide gel in 0.5x TBE buffer, followed by phosphorimaging.
Site-directed mapping at H2B53-DNA contacts

Histone octamers with cysteine at residue 53 of H2B were conjugated to p-azidophenacyl bromide immediately after octamer refolding. Reactions contained 80 nM WT or mutant Arp5 complexes and 80 nM nucleosomes and were incubated at 30 C for 30 min in conditions. Nucleosome movement was initiated by adding 80 muM ATP and stopped with 300 ng/mul sonicated salmon sperm DNA and 10 mM EDTA at the indicated time points. For site-directed histone-DNA crosslinking, samples were irradiated with UV for 3 min (310 nm, 2.65 mW/cm2). Samples were denatured with 0.1% SDS at 37 C for 20 min in 30 mM NaCl and 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0). Crosslinked protein-DNA were enriched and separated from un-crosslinked DNA by phenol-chloroform (4:1) extraction. The aqueous phase containing un-crosslinked DNA was discarded. Crosslinked DNA was ethanol precipitated with 1M LiCl in the presence of sheared salmon sperm DNA as carrier. Crosslinked DNA was cleaved with 1 M pyrrolidine (Sigma) at 90 C for 15 min. DNA samples were analyzed alongside a sequence ladder made from the same DNA on a denaturing 6.5% polyacrylamide gels containing 8 M urea. Gels were visualized by phosphorimaging and quantified using ImageQuant software (Version 5.2). Data images in figures are representative of n = 3 experiments. %Net loss of signal for WT or mutants on the entry side was calculated using formula  where X0 is the crosslinking at time 0 s and Xt is the crosslinking at time t.
AlphaFold2 modeling of Sc Arp5

The AlphaFold2 predicted structure for Sc Arp5 comes from the AlphaFold Structure Database of EMBL-EBI and is AF-P53946-F1 model v4_1. This structure was last updated in AlphaFold DB version 2022-11-01 and created with the AlphaFold Monomer v2.0 pipeline. The confidence of the structure is shown using the predicted local difference test (pLDDT) and most of the grappler domain has pLDDT scores ranging from 70 to 90 in the high-confidence range, see Supplementary Figure S4A. The AlphaFold2 structure of Sc Arp5 is aligned using Pymol 2.5.4 from Schrodinger, LLC to the Ct Arp5 structure that was obtained using a combination of cryo-EM and AlphaFold2 modeling to confirm the overall similarity between the two structures, see Supplementary Figure S4B (9).
Results
An arginine anchor in the grappler domain is required for INO80 mobilizing nucleosomes and for Arp5 contacting the acidic pocket of nucleosomes

The cryo-EM structures of Ct and Sc INO80 coupled with AlphaFold2 modeling have provided evidence for a putative arginine anchor in the grappler domain of Arp5 that interacts with the acidic pocket of nucleosomes. The functional role of this putative arginine anchor has unfortunately not been experimentally validated for Sc Arp5 and prompted us to mutate three conserved arginines in the 'foot' and 'leg' regions of Sc Arp5. Arg 482 is conserved in Sc and D. melanogaster but in S. pombe and T. thermophilia is replaced by Lys and Arg 488 and Arg 496 in Sc Arp5 are well conserved up to D. melanogaster (Figure 1A). Mutating these three arginines to alanine greatly reduced the nucleosome mobilizing activity of INO80 and its ATPase activity is reduced 4-fold without altering the complex integrity of INO80 (Supplementary Figures S1A-C and S7A and Table 1). These arginines are shown to be important for Arp5 to contact the surface proximal to the nucleosome acidic pocket as seen when mutating them to alanine reduces Arp5 crosslinking to modified residue 89 of histone H2A to 23% of that observed with WT (Figure 1D). The arginine anchor of Sc Arp5 is important for Arp5 binding the acidic pocket and INO80 mobilizing nucleosomes.

The arginine anchor of Arp5 is required for binding the acidic pocket of nucleosomes and mobilizing nucleosomes. (A) The conserved arginines and lysines located in the 'leg' and 'foot' regions of Arp5 are shown. (B and C) These graphs show (B) nucleosome mobilizing and (C) ATPase activities for INO80 containing wild type (WT) or mutant Arp5 (Arp5R3) with Arg 482, 488 and 491 mutated to Ala. Remodeling and ATPase assays had 50 nM 70N5 601 nucleosomes, 75 nM INO80 and 80 muM ATP. The ATPase activity is assayed using gamma-32P-ATP and thin layer chromatography. (D and E) The interactions of Arp5 near the acidic pocket of nucleosomes at residue 89 of H2A is assayed by site-specific histone crosslinking. A representative phosphorimage of the 4-20% SDS-PAGE is shown in (D) and the bar graph in (E) shows the changes in photoaffinity labeling between WT and Arp5R3 complexes. There are a total of three replicates and error bars represent the mean +- SD. (F) The in vivo effect of mutating Arp5's arginine anchor is assayed using growth spot assays and the AA system to acutely test cell viability under conditions that INO80 is required, see also Supplementary Figure S1B. DMSO: demethylsulfoxide; RAPA: rapamycin (3 mug/ml). In panel (F) (top panel), cells were plated on -URACIL synthetic media (bottom panel) cells were plated on YEPD medium. Rapamycin concentration is 3 mug/ml.

The in vivo role of the arginine anchor of Arp5 is tested using the AA method to determine if mutant versions of Arp5 can compensate for the acute removal of WT Arp5 and avoid cells adapting after prolonged exposure to mutant Arp5. WT Arp5 is shown to be vital for INO80's role in response to DNA replication stress caused by hydroxyurea (HU), heat/cold stress and transcription of the INO1 gene, all of which is rescued by ectopic expression of Arp5 (Supplementary Figure S1B). The arginine anchor of Arp5 and its regulation of the nucleosome mobilizing activity of INO80 is however not the critical activity of INO80 required for alleviating DNA replication stress (HU) or facilitating in DNA repair (MMS) and potentially transcription elongation (6-azauracil; 6-AU) (Figure 1F).

To better understand the role of the arginine anchor for INO80 remodeling, we examine DNA movement on the two sides of the nucleosome and DNA displacement on the entry side by site-directed histone-DNA crosslinking (Figure 2A). We focus on early DNA movement and the most prominent steps of 32 and 20 bp at the exit and entry sides of nucleosomes. DNA movement on the entry side of nucleosomes is observed in a limited number of nucleosomes (12%), stops after only 40 s and subsequently decreases (Figure 2B; Supplementary Figure S2). DNA movement of 32 bp on the exit side is more prominent than on the entry side as it occurs in nearly half of all nucleosomes in the time window of 160 s (Figure 2B). Mutation of the arginine anchor strongly blocks early DNA movement on both sides of the nucleosome (Figure 2C and D). In the same early time window, INO80 displaces DNA from the histone octamer as seen by a net loss of histone-DNA crosslinking on the entry side that is not dramatically changed by mutating the arginine anchor (Figure 2E). In summary, early DNA movement on both sides of the nucleosome is severely impact by mutating the arginine anchor but not early DNA displacement on the entry side.

Early during INO80 remodeling the arginine anchor of Arp5 is required for DNA movement on both sides of nucleosomes, but not for DNA displacement on the entry side. (A) The approach for mapping DNA movement and displacement inside of nucleosomes by histone-DNA crosslinking is depicted. Arrows indicate where histone crosslinks to DNA before and during remodeling or is absent. Evidence for two alternative conformations of the Arp5 grappler domain binding to nucleosomes

We probe the interactions of the Arp5 subunit with nucleosomes by crosslinking INO80 to specific histone sites on the surface of the nucleosome. Seven different photoreactive nucleosomes are constructed with histone octamers that have an 125I labeled photoreactive reporter at positions in the lateral surface of the octamer and the radiolabel is transferred by crosslinking to the proximal subunit(s) of INO80 (Supplementary Figure S3A). Arp5 is the major subunit of INO80 that is crosslinked to the octamer face, primarily at residues 89 and 80 of histones H2A and H3 that are respectively located on the edge of the nucleosomal acidic pocket and adjacent to Arp5's DNA binding domain (Figure 3A and B; Supplementary Figure S3B and C). The pattern of Arp5 crosslinking is consistent with INO80's cryo-EM structure.

Site-specific histone crosslinking reveals two distinct modes of Arp5 binding to the acidic patch of nucleosomes important for INO80 remodeling. (A) The hemagglutitin epitope (HA) is fused to the C-terminus of Arp5 subunit to aid in peptide mapping and purified INO80 with and without Arp5 HA tagged are analyzed on a 4-20% SDS-PAGE and stained with Coomassie blue. (B) Photoaffinity labeling of WT and HA-tagged Arp5 is shown at two histone positions, residues 89 of histone H2A (H2A89) and 80 of histone H3 (H380). A representative phosphorimage of a 4-20% SDS-PAGE is shown. (C) The structural organization of the 'cross' conformation of the Sc Arp5 subunit generated by AlphaFold2 is shown and the regions crosslinked to H2A89 and H380 (see also Supplementary Figure S4C). (D) Residues 516-565 and 565-620 are crosslinked to residue 89 of histone H2A; whereas (E) residues 385-515 of Arp5 crosslink to residue 80 of histone H3 and the crosslinked regions are highlighted. (F and G) Graphs show the (F) nucleosome mobilizing and (G) ATPase activities of Arp5 and Arp5Delta516-564 complexes and the error bars show the mean +- SD with 3 replicates (see also Supplementary Figure S5C). (H) The interactions of Arp5 with the histone octamer face of nucleosomes are probed by site-specific histone crosslinking for WT and mutant Arp5Delta516-564 (see Supplementary Figure S5B). The relative efficiency of crosslinking for Arp5, Ies2 and Ies6 is shown for three replicates and error bars represent the mean +- SD.

The region(s) of Arp5 contacting nucleosomes at these two sites are determined by immobilizing photoaffinity labeled Arp5 through its C-terminal end, cleaving with Arg-C and removing the proteolytic fragments not immobilized, and analyzing the C-terminal fragments by SDS-PAGE (Figure 3C; Supplementary Figure S3D-F). A set of Arp5 specific molecular weight markers combined with phosphorimaging determines where the crosslink is located (Supplementary Figure S3D and E). There are two regions of Arp5 corresponding to amino acids 516 to 564 and 565 to 620 that are crosslinked to residue 89 of histone H2A (Figure 3C; Supplementary Figure S3F). The two regions are detected under single-hit cleavage conditions and with more extensive digestion (Supplementary Figure S3F, left side, lanes 2 versus 4). When crosslinking is switched to residue 80 of histone H3, the cleavage pattern changes and reveals crosslinking primarily to amino acids 358 to 516 of Arp5 (Supplementary Figure S3F, right side).

The grappler domain has been observed to be dynamic with a minimum of two alternative conformations by cryo-EM. The two conformations include the previously described 'cross' and 'parallel' conformations and there is currently no structural model available for the 'parallel' version. The spatial arrangement of the regions of Arp5 crosslinked to the two locations on the open histone octamer face are visualized using a structural model of Sc Arp5 bound to nucleosomes based on the cryo-EM structure Ct INO80 and modeling using AlphaFold2 (Figure 3D and E). In the Sc INO80 model, most of Sc Arp5 is modeled with high confidence (>70 pLDDT) and correlates well to the cryo-EM structure of Ct Arp5 in the 'cross' configuration (Supplementary Figures S4A and B). We observe using this model that the region from amino acids 516 to 564 is proximal to residues 89 of H2A, consistent with our crosslinking, and is located proximal to the putative arginine anchor of Arp5 that is likely responsible for Arp5 binding the acid pocket of nucleosomes (Figure 3D). Surprisingly, the other region from amino acids 565 to 620 is not proximal to residue 89 of H2A and its crosslinking pattern is inconsistent with the 'cross' conformation model (Figure 3D). These data suggest two alternative conformations of Arp5 potentially engage the histone octamer which are both detected by histone crosslinking.

The crosslinking pattern at residue 80 of histone H3 also indicates two distinct ways that the grappler domain binds to the octamer face. The region from amino acids 386 to 515 based on the 'cross' grappler conformation of Arp5 is expected to crosslink to residue 89 of H2A, which is detected to a lesser extent, however this region is more prominently crosslinked to residue 80 of histone H3 (Figure 3C and E, the orange highlighted region; Supplementary Figure S3F). Our data suggest that the site-specific histone to Arp5 crosslinking reveals two distinct conformations of the grappler domain with one corresponding to the 'cross' conformation and the other a conformation that has likely not been previously reported.
The two alternative conformations of the grappler domain of Arp5 have distinct functions

The functional significance of the different conformations of the grappler domain are first examined by separately deleting each of the two regions shown to be proximal to the acidic pocket of nucleosomes. INO80 complex integrity is maintained when amino acids 516-564 (Arp5Delta516-564) are deleted, but when amino acids 565-620 (Arp5Delta565-620) are deleted Ies6 and Arp5 are not stably assembled into the complex (Supplementary Figure S5A). Previously, deletion of parts of Arp5 in the grappler domain had been shown to disrupt complex integrity similar to that observed here and the Arp5Delta565-620 complex is not analyzed further for this reason. The mutant Arp5Delta516-564 INO80 complex is more defective than the Arp5R3 complex for mobilizing nucleosomes even though they have comparable rate of ATP hydrolysis, respectively 0.34 and 0.27 nM/s (compare Figure 1B and C with Figure 3F and G; Supplementary Figure S5C and Table 1). The reduction of Arp5 interactions near the acidic pocket is not significantly different between the Arp5Delta516-564 deletion and Arp5R3 complex as seen by crosslinking to residue 89 of H2A (compare Figure 1E to Figure 3H; see also Supplementary Figure S5B).

The Arp5Delta516-564 mutant is phenotypically equivalent to the absence of Arp5 and is highly defective for normal INO80 function in heat stress response, DNA replication stress and transcription elongation unlike that observed for the Arp5R3 mutant (compare Figure 4A with Figure 1F). The different growth defects of Arp5Delta516-564 and Arp5R3 suggest there are additional defects caused by the deletion than merely disrupting the interactions of the arginine anchor and therefore prompted further characterization of this region of Arp5. Several residues between amino acid 514 and 571 are conserved in fungi and flies but not in mammals (Figure 4B). Small clusters of these residues are mutated to alanine and then tested using our AA system as described before (Figure 4B and C). We found Leu 567, Leu 568 and Asp 571 mutated to Ala is the only one of five clusters that is defective for INO80 in DNA replication stress, DNA damage repair and transcription elongation (Figure 4C). We also mutated Arg residues either conserved in the regions from 565 to 620 or the brace part of the grappler domain at residues 301, 307 and 316 and found when mutated to Ala do not have a INO80 defect like that observed for Leu 567, Leu 668 and Asp 571 (see Supplementary Figure S6A-E).

The phenotype of Arp5LLD is not as severe as Arp5Delta516-564 as seen by varying the concentration of HU with 100 mM not showing any growth defects with Arp5LLD but is lethal for Arp5Delta516-564 (Figure 4A and Supplementary S6F). Mutating both the arginine anchor and LLD region has a phenotype that more closely resemble the HU sensitivity of Arp5Delta516-564 and points to the severe defect with the deletion mutant being due to eliminating the interactions of both conformations of Arp5 with nucleosomes (Supplementary Figure S6). When the DBD mutant is combined with the arginine anchor or LLD region mutants, we observe a similar HU sensitive lethality that either alone does not have (Supplementary Figure S6). These results suggest the DBD domain might also be important for the function of the grappler domain.

Mutations in the LLD or DBD region or the combination of both do not change the complex integrity of INO80 or affinity for nucleosomes compared with WT Arp5 (Supplementary Figures S7A and S8A-D). The more severe phenotype for the Arp5LLD versus Arp5R3 complex is apparently not due to nucleosome mobilization being more impaired because Arp5LLD mobilizes nucleosomes more efficiently than Arp5R3 (Figure 5A; Supplementary Figure S7B). The ATPase activity of Arp5LLD is also nearly 2-fold faster than the Arp5R3 complex (Supplementary Figure S7C; Table 1). The LLD region facilitates Arp5 binding to histone octamer face much like the arginine anchor, consistent with two alternate grappler domain conformations engaging this surface (Figure 5A compared with Figure 1E).

Leu 567, Leu 568 and Asp 571 (LLD) is required for binding H2A-H2B dimers, Arp5 binding to the acidic pocket of nucleosomes and INO80 mobilizing nucleosomes. (A) The nucleosome remodeling activity of WT and mutant Arp5LLD, Arp5DBD and Arp5R3 complexes are measured using EMSA and the extent of mobilized nucleosome plotted versus time (see also Supplementary Figure S7B). (B) Relative histone crosslinking efficiency is plotted for Arp5 near the acid pocket (H2A89) and another lateral position on the histone octamer (H380) for WT and mutant Arp5LLD, Arp5DBD and Arp5LLD+DBD (see also Supplementary Figure S8C). (C and D) Pulldown assays are done with (C) nucleosomes and (D) H2A/B dimer using biotinylated LANA peptide and WT and mutant Arp5 Arg anchor and LLD peptides. DNA in the nucleosomes is P32 radiolabeled and is also tracked in the nucleosome pulldown assays as shown in the lower panel of (C). (E) Nucleosomes are preincubated with 6, 18 and 50 muM of LANA, WT or mutant LLD peptides for 30 min before adding 75 nM INO80 and incubating for 30 min. Remodeling reactions are stopped 10 min after addition of 80 muM ATP and analyzed on a 5% native polyacrylamide gel.

The DBD domain binds DNA close to where the grappler domain binds and could tether the grappler domain to the nucleosome, which would be consistent with the earlier phenotype observed when mutating the DBD domain and either the arginine anchor or LLD region (Supplementary Figure S6F). The DNA binding activity of DBD alone does not dictate whether the grappler domain binds to the lateral face of nucleosomes as seen by no reduction in Arp5 crosslinking to residue 89 of H2A or 80 of H3 with the Arp5DBD compared with WT complex (Figure 5B). DBD binding DNA at SHL-2/-3 is required however to tether the grappler domain to the lateral surface of the nucleosome when the interactions of the LLD are disrupted as shown by histone crosslinking (Figure 5B; Supplementary Figure S8E). Mutation of LLD alone reduces the crosslinking of Arp5 at H2A89 to 23% of WT and to 46% of WT at H380, and when combined with mutation of DBD the crosslinking at H2A89 and H380 is reduced to only 7-8%. These data suggest  DBD could have an important tethering function for the grappler domain when one conformation of the grappler domain releases its contact and rotates to the other conformation. If the grappler domain rotates to the conformation and is unable to bind the nucleosome surface, then the grappler domain would be prone to dissociate and thereby lose its ability to rotate back to the starting conformation.

Biotinylated LLD and arginine anchor peptides are used in pulldown assays to determine whether these parts of Arp5 can independently bind to the acidic patch of nucleosomes or free histone H2A-H2B dimers. In comparison to the prototypical arginine anchor of LANA, the Arp5 arginine anchor binds weakly to nucleosomes but is nonetheless specific as seen by the loss of binding when the arginines corresponding to residue 482, 488 and 496 of Arp5 are mutated to alanine (Figure 5C). The preferred binding target for LLD is the free H2A-H2B dimer with a higher affinity for the dimer than either the LANA or R3 peptide and does not detectably bind nucleosomes and presumably the acidi patch (Figure 5C and D). These results indicate that the LLD region likely recognizes the part of the H2A-H2B dimer either bound to DNA or the H3-H4 tetramer due to its lack of interactions with nucleosomes. The LLD peptide was further confirmed to not bind nucleosomes at the acidic patch based on the LLD peptide not interfering with INO80 remodeling like the LANA peptide (Figure 5E). Binding of the LLD peptide to H2A-H2B is dependent on Leu 567, Leu 568 and Asp 571 as shown by reducing 4-fold the amount of dimer pulled down when changed to alanine (Figure 5D). The dimer specificity of LLD suggests this region could be involved in dimer exchange, which is consistent with Arp5LLD being defective for DNA replication where INO80 needs to replace H2A.Z with H2A.

The LLD residues are located at one end of an alpha-helix that associates by way of a leucine zipper with the 'leg' helix (Figure 6A-C and 3C; Supplementary Figure S4C). Disruption of the interactions between these two helices potentially could affect binding of the arginine anchor since the 'leg' helix is attached to where the anchor resides in the 'foot' region. Mutation of Leu 567 and Leu 568 is expected however to not disturb the leucine zipper holding these two alpha helixes together, based on its location at the extreme end of the zipper and the maintenance of five Leu-Leu or Leu-Ile pairs and two ionic pairs crucial in the helix-helix interactions (Figure 6B and C). Protein modeling with AlphaFold3 also confirms no change is predicted in the tertiary structure of the grappler domain when Leu 567, Leu 568 and Asp 571 are mutated to Ala (Figure 6D). Mutation of LLD is therefore expected to not impact binding of the arginine anchor to the acidic pocket.

(A-C) Models showing the composition and placement of residues in the 'arm', 'foot' and 'leg' regions of the grappler domain along with the average distances between key residues. (D) Shown are the structural models generated by AlphaFold3 of Arp5's grappler domain for WT and mutated LLD, that illustrate no predicted change in the grappler domain due to mutation of Leu 567 and 568 and Glu 571 to Ala.

The stage(s) of INO80 remodeling impacted by mutation of LLD is determined by mapping DNA movement and displacement as described earlier. The initial rate of DNA movement by Arp5LLD on the exit side of nucleosomes is reduced 4-fold compared with WT but is overall 6.5-fold more active than Arp5R3 with DNA moving 2.7-fold faster and occurring in 2.4-fold more nucleosomes (Figure 7A-B and Table 1). Like Arp5R3, the Arp5DBD complex is also more defective moving DNA on the exit side than Arp5LLD (Figure 7A and B and Table 1). In contrast, the Arp5LLD complex on the entry side moves DNA less than Arp5R3 and Arp5DBD as seen by the reduced rate in the loss of the starting DNA contact (Figure 7C). Furthermore, Arp5LLD displaces DNA from the histone octamer 2- to 4-fold less than Arp5R3, Arp5DBD and WT and after only 20 s stops displacing DNA (Figure 7D). The LLD region appears to have a more critical role for moving and displacing DNA from the histone octamer on the entry side than DNA movement on the exit side.

The LLD patch of Arp5 is most critical for DNA movement and displacement on the entry side of nucleosomes. (A-D) DNA movement is tracked on the (A and B) exit and (C) entry sides of nucleosomes using a photoreactive probe attached to residue 53 of histone H2B and (D) DNA displacement on the entry side with INO80 containing WT Arp5 and mutant Arp5DBD, Arp5LLD and Arp5R3 as indicated. The movement of (A and B) 32 bp on the exit side and (C) the loss of the initial crosslinking position on the entry side is plotted versus time with graph (B) showing the reactions over a more extended time. In (D), the net loss of DNA crosslinking on the entry side is plotted. Three replicates are performed for each condition and error bars represent the mean +- SD.
Discussion

We have identified a region of the Arp5 subunit of INO80 required in vitro and in vivo for INO80 remodeling activity that binds free H2A-H2B dimers, associates with the lateral face of nucleosomes and is potentially involved in H2A/H2A.Z dimer exchange by INO80. A peptide spanning residues 557 to 581 of Arp5 binds free H2A-H2B dimers that is dependent on a short acidic hydrophobic patch consisting of Leu 567, Leu 568 and Asp 571 (LLD). The surface of the H2A-H2B dimer bound by this region does not correspond to the region normally exposed in nucleosomes as the peptide is unable to bind nucleosomes or inhibit INO80 remodeling as does an arginine anchor. Nonetheless, this region is bound in the vicinity of the acidic pocket of nucleosomes in an LLD dependent manner and is required for stable binding of the grappler domain. The LLD region could bind to the surface of dimers exposed either due to INO80 binding that lifts DNA off the H2A-H2B consistent with the cryo-EM structure of INO80 nucleosome and/or DNA being lifted off the dimer by INO80 during nucleosome remodeling. Interestingly, we observe the LLD mutant has the most pronounced adverse impact on INO80 remodeling at the stage of DNA displacement. H2A.Z is specifically replaced by H2A on the same entry side of nucleosomes where mutation of LLD interferes with DNA displacement as shown using 3-color single molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer, consistent with earlier biochemical data. These data point to the LLD region having the ability to promote DNA lifting  off the histone octamer in a manner tied to binding the normally excluded surface of H2A-H2B and potentially links the LLD region to dimer exchange.

The connection of the LLD region to INO80 replacing H2A.Z with H2A is further validated based on in vivo assays examining the response to DNA replication stress using HU. INO80 has also been shown in vivo to replace H2A.Z with H2A in homologous recombination, maintenance of genome integrity, normal DNA replication and recovery from replication stress. INO80 facilitates in the response to DNA replication stress by removing H2A.Z in order to resolve R-loops formed by replication forks colliding with transcription complexes. In this study, we find that mutation of LLD produces an HU or DNA replication stress-sensitive phenotype consistent with the LLD region being required for the dimer exchange activity of INO80. Although mutation of LLD also reduces the nucleosome mobilizing activity of INO80, it is not likely the reason for its HU-sensitivity since mutation of the arginine anchor of Arp5 is not HU-sensitive even though it severely inhibits INO80 nucleosome mobilizing activity more than mutation of LLD.

Structural modeling of the grappler domain bound to the lateral face of the histone octamer highlights that the LLD region and arginine anchor cannot simultaneously bind to the same region of the nucleosomes and are on opposite faces of the grappler domain. Site-specific histone-Arp5 crosslinking and peptide mapping reveals the grappler domain binds nucleosomes in two different conformations, one in which the arginine anchor is bound to the acidic pocket and the other with the LLD region associated nearby. We validate that both regions are bound to the lateral face of nucleosomes by mutation of the arginine anchor and the LLD residues equally diminishing Arp5 interactions near the acidic pocket. Mutation of the LLD region is not expected to perturb binding of the arginine anchor based on structural constraints and modeling and therefore the loss of grappler domain binding with mutant LLD is most likely a direct effect.

The two-conformation model of the grappler domain suggests that dimer exchange by INO80 may involve switching the grappler domain surface engaged with nucleosomes. Given the properties of the LLD region, LLD could bind a free H2A-H2B dimer and then rotate into the position where it could switch out the H2A.Z-H2B for H2A-H2B dimer. We find the grappler domain is likely prone to releasing its contact with the nucleosome face, based on the relatively weak binding of the arginine anchor of Arp5 to the acid pocket and the lack of the LLD region binding alone to nucleosomes. The transient binding of the grappler domain to nucleosomes would facilitate in the dynamic switching back and forth of its binding interface.

Other evidence consistent with the dynamic shifting of the grappler domain comes by investigating the potential role of the DBD domain binding DNA at SHL-2 and -3 coupled to shifting of the grappler domain. We observe that mutation of DBD alone does not reduce binding of the grappler domain either at the acidic pocket or near residue 80 of H3 proximal, but when combined with the LLD mutant there is a dramatic loss of grappler domain binding that is much greater than either mutation alone. These data suggest the DBD domain is necessary to tether the grappler domain when the binding of one conformation of the grappler is reduced. Although there may be several reasons for this observation, it seems plausible that the DBD domain could become critical for the grappler when in the process of switching between conformations one of them is unable to bind. In this situation the loss of DBD binding to DNA would cause a greater tendency for the grappler to dissociate from the nucleosome and thereby be unable to switch back. With this in mind, it is interesting to point out the loss of both LLD and arginine anchor binding to nucleosomes is phenotypically similar to the combined mutation of LDD and DBD consistent with the proposed model.

passages.text: Efficacy and Safety Profile of Biosimilar Polyethylene Glycol (PEG)-Asparaginase (Asviia) in Patients With Acute Leukemia: A Retrospective Study From Kashmir

Background: Biosimilar pegylated L-asparaginase offers a promising alternative to the innovator molecule for treating acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in Indian children. It addresses challenges associated with drug availability and cost while providing similar therapeutic advantages. This biosimilar ensures wider access to essential treatment in resource-limited settings such as India.

Materials and methods: A retrospective study was conducted at the Pediatric Oncology unit of the Department of Medical Oncology, Sher-I-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences (SKIMS) Srinagar. The study evaluated the efficacy and safety of biosimilar polyethylene glycol-asparaginase (PEG-ASP) (Asviia) in newly diagnosed pediatric ALL patients treated between January 2021 and December 2023. Each patient received two induction doses of PEG-ASP.

Results: The study included 45 patients (29 boys, 16 girls) with a median age of 7.5 years (range: 1-16 years), with most patients diagnosed with Pre-B ALL. The median PEG-ASP dose administered intravenously was 1175 IU (range: 1125-3750 IU). Significant improvements in hemoglobin and platelet counts were observed following the first dose of PEG-ASP. The biosimilar PEG-ASP was well tolerated, with no life-threatening events reported. At the end of the induction phase, 40 patients (88.89%) achieved complete remission with minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity, while five patients had MRD positivity.

Conclusion: The study provides valuable insights into the efficacy and safety of biosimilar PEG-ASP for pediatric ALL in resource-limited settings, with strong data on remission rates and minimal adverse events.
Introduction

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) constitutes nearly 77% of all cancers diagnosed in children under 15 years of age globally . In India, leukemia accounts for approximately 40 to 50% of the total childhood cancer burden, with ALL being the most prevalent type with an incidence rate of up to 101.4 per million in boys and 62.3 per million in girls . Chemotherapy remains the main treatment for pediatric ALL worldwide, with high-income countries achieving a 5-year overall survival rate of around 90% through effective protocols like Children's Oncology Group (COG) and Berlin-Frankfurt-Munster (BFM), while India shows progress but still lags with survival rates ranging from 45% to 81% due to challenges in uniform treatment, supportive care, and treatment abandonment . Currently, there are three asparaginase preparations available: L-asparaginase (native asparaginase), polyethylene glycol-asparaginase (PEG-ASP) (Asviia) derived from Escherichia coli, and Erwinia asparaginase sourced from Erwinia chrysanthemi . PEG-ASP received FDA approval in February 1994 for intramuscular use in patients with ALL who have hypersensitivity to native forms of L-asparaginase. In November 2005, the FDA approved the intravenous administration of PEG-ASP, and in July 2006, expanded its approval for frontline treatment of ALL patients based on the COG study CCG-1962 . PEG-ASP is the preferred formulation in ALL treatment regimens because of its longer half-life, which extends the circulation time of the enzyme and minimizes immunogenicity compared to native asparaginase .

PEG-ASP is a bioengineered compound synthesized through the covalent linkage between E. coli-L-asparaginase (EC-ASP) and PEG units. This innovative process, known as PEGylation, involves the modification of biological molecules by the non-toxic and non-immunogenic polymer, PEG . The strategic application of PEGylation allows for the optimization of enzyme activity by facilitating unhindered access to the enzyme's active sites, while concurrently impeding the uptake of EC-ASP by the reticuloendothelial system . PEG-ASP has a longer half-life and lower immunogenicity than unmodified EC-ASP, enabling sustained asparagine depletion with fewer allergic reactions. This allows for less frequent dosing and fewer interruptions in ALL treatment. Additionally, PEG-ASP is more thermally stable and less temperature-dependent, facilitating easier transport and storage, which enhances accessibility in varied clinical settings. This dual mechanism not only enhances the therapeutic efficacy of ASP but also shields its antigenic determinants from immune recognition, thereby reducing the possibility of antibody development . Leukemia cells require exogenous asparagine to survive, while normal cells can synthesize asparagine. Asparaginase depletes serum asparagine by converting it to aspartic acid and ammonia. Therefore, this anti-leukemic activity causes deprivation of the critical amino acid, leading to cell death .

In addition to its therapeutic benefits, the administration of Asviia in pediatric ALL treatment regimens requires a comprehensive understanding of its associated toxicities. Reported adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypersensitivity reactions, all of which can significantly impact patient outcomes and treatment adherence . Recognizing the importance of potential risks associated with PEG-ASP, our study evaluates the efficacy of PEG-ASP and its associated toxicities in pediatric ALL patients within the Indian population.
